title: Aussie teen revving to take on world's best in sim racing championships
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Xavier Cain may well be the only teenager looking forward to his alarm going off at 3 o'clock on a Monday morning.

The 16-year-old student from Mount Gambier, in south-eastern South Australia, will be jumping out of bed and into the driver's seat as he competes against some of the world's best simulator racers.

From the comfort of his home, Xavier will take on other sim racers in the 2026 Porsche eSports Super Cup World Championship, with competition getting underway at 4am on Monday.

"I'm not really aiming to finish a certain position, but I definitely just want to learn a lot for this year," Xavier said.

Xavier's set-up at his home will help him take on some of the best simulator drivers in the world. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I'm hoping I can be back for many years to come, so I'm not too worried about trying to finish well.

"I just really want to learn a lot so I can bring it into the future years to come."

The Porsche Cup prize is a hefty one: $US10,000 and the chance to compete for a real-world development driving spot with the German motorsport giant.

Racing simulators use computer screens, a realistic steering wheel, and pedal set-ups. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I always had hopes that I could do well," Xavier said.

" About a year ago, I had a conversation with my friend, and it was just a 'what if' conversation, like how good it would be to race in a world championship. "

Talent on show

Simulation racing uses computers and a realistic pedal and steering-wheel system to create a lifelike driving experience.

Racers need to consider real-world variables like tyre wear, vehicle damage and fuel levels as they tear around virtual tracks.

Driving on the simulator program iRacing, Xavier quickly rose through the rankings and joined a professional team, Automoves Racing, just six months ago.

He is now in the top 1 per cent of racers on iRacing.

Co-owner Jordan McDonnell said Xavier's talent was clear and he was fast-tracked from the academy to the main team.

Jordan McDonnell is a sim racer and sprint car driver. (Supplied: Automoves Racing)

"Even though his ranking was a lot lower than what was needed to be in our main team, I spoke to the other owner and made an exception for him to be able to be pushed up," Mr McDonnell said.

" One thing's led to another and now he's in the top 32 in the world for Porsche Cup cars and representing us on a global stage. "

Based in New Zealand, Mr McDonnell was a sprint car racer before founding his e-sport team with the help of a friend in Canada he met online through sim racing.

He said sim racing had helped grow motorsport and allowed more people access to what could be an expensive industry.

Professional Indycar driver Scott McLaughlin is also boosting the sim racing scene. (Supplied: Twitch)

"There was a driver that was in the academy, his name's Nicholas, and we promoted him to the main team not too long ago," Mr McDonnell said.

"It's 2 in the morning in Poland where he's from, and he just starts yelling out of joy, waking his whole family up.

"So hearing that and his reaction and waking his parents up at 2am, getting promoted … that really just makes you feel good and makes you feel part of something bigger."

Making motorsport accessible

Racing simulators have long been used by motorsport teams as a way for drivers to practice their skills, but they remained a niche hobby for amateurs.

In the past decade, however, sim racing has exploded in popularity as the technology has become more accessible and social media has given it a platform.

Big motorsport names like Formula One champion Max Verstappen, who has formed his own sim racing team to compete in global events, have also helped to push the e-sport into the mainstream.

Major events are governed by international motorsport's peak body the FIA.

Formula 1 driver Max Verstappen has formed his own sim racing team to compete in global events. (Getty Images: EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto, Marcel van Dorst)

Melbourne driver and content creator Emily Jones said the online culture around sim racing enabled her to have a career in motorsport.

"I've raced against Max Verstappen, Shane Van Gisbergen and Scott McLaughlin and all these international fantastic racing drivers," she said.

" That opportunity wouldn't have happened if it wasn't for sim racing. "

Emily Jones turned her real-world racing experience into success in the virtual world. (Supplied: Emily Jones)

Ms Jones now streams her racing to about 38,000 subscribers on Twitch and produces videos for a YouTube channel dedicated to the e-sport.

"I've been lucky enough to travel overseas multiple times to Germany, Poland, Japan, the US and lots of really interesting places to both compete in international competitions and also just to create content around sim racing," she said.

" If I could go back and tell a child version of myself that I get to travel and also get paid to essentially play advanced video games, I would be pretty stoked. "

Early mornings ahead

Back in Mount Gambier, Xavier's early wake-ups will continue for the next six weeks as he starts his world championship campaign.

It won't be easy juggling the high-octane competition with Year 11 classes at school and TAFE, where he is studying automotive service and technology.

But mum Teresa Cain will be cheering him on as he chases a world title and a chance at a dream real-world experience.

Xavier and his mum, Teresa, are bracing for the early morning race starts as part of the world championship. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"That's everyone's dream that's in racing, isn't it?" she said.

"It would be just amazing to see him get from this and get to that level.

"We'll give him the best possible chance we can and tick all the right boxes to hopefully get him there."

title: Maths doesn't add up for Australian parents juggling work and school
text:
Australian families are living in work, school and care systems designed for another era. And the math ain't mathing.

Morning scramble. Uniform. Lunch box. Breakfast. Hair. Teeth. Socks. Socks! Drop off. Commute to work. Work. Pick-up. After school sport. The assemblies. The parades. The homework. The appointments. The pings of parent WhatsApp groups. The bottomless laundry basket. The shopping. The dinner. The never-ending list of unpaid work. The endless worry and guilt.

When it comes to working and being a modern-day parent, the juggle is real.

If we look back to family life in the 1960s, or even the 1990s, so much has changed.

In most two-parent families these days, both parents are employed, but the work and school systems are largely set up for a bygone era.

"The maths does not add up," says Kate Harrison Brennan, director of the Sydney Policy Lab at The University of Sydney.

To help us put the numbers in context and talk about real solutions, alongside Dr Harrison Brennan we've enlisted these experts:

Elizabeth Hill from The University of Sydney Department of Political Economy

Georgie Dent, CEO of advocacy organisation The Parenthood

Lyndall Strazdins from the ANU National Centre of Epidemiology and Population Health

Rowena Ditzell, lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney

So with the introductions out of the way, let's do some rough sums.

The maths

Parents can feel like there aren't enough hours in the day. And when you stop to work out just how much overlap there is between the hours that your children need you, and the hours that you're expected to devote to work, it's easy to see why.

We know that every family arrangement is different.

Let's assume there are two parents at home, and both parents work full-time.

We're going to look specifically at parents of primary school-aged children and compare the average work year with the average school year.

7.5 hours per week Is the gap between the full-time work week and average primary school hours. Read more Read more School often starts about 9am and finishes between 3pm and 3:30pm. The traditional full-time work day is 9am to 5pm or 8 hours. Assuming school finishes at 3:30pm, that's 300 hours per year parents need to find across the 40-week school year. "What becomes immediately obvious for any parent in the first week of their child being at school is that suddenly there is a cliff when you get to 2 something in the afternoon … and kids need to get picked up," Dr Harrison Brennan says. After-school care is often relied upon to cover the gap, but that's if parents can afford it. It gets expensive if you have multiple children. And many people don't have access to it at all. "I'd say you're part of a lucky one in five in Australia," Dr Harrison Brennan says. "The reality is: places in subsidised after-school-hours care are incredibly concentrated in Australia's major cities." "The gap between care and work, and school hours and work hours, isn't an inconvenience; it's a structural tax that parents, most often mums, pay every single day," says The Parenthood CEO Georgie Dent.

3.8 hours per week For the average commute to work. Read more Read more The average daily commute is 52 minutes, or about 56 minutes in capital cities. On average, Australians spend 3.8 hours commuting to work each week, which is about 182 hours per year. While many Australians are now able to work from home, or work a hybrid arrangement, most Australian workers still commute to work. "For those who work at a distance from their workplace and from their school drop-off, the degree of difficulty in completing that task every day, five days a week, for four terms a year is really, really high," Professor Hill says. The COVID-19 pandemic did make working from home much more common. It's one of the things that's made the workplace happier for many women, Dr Strazdins says. "They're finding that time by cutting back on a commute from work, from home and dovetailing tasks a bit better," she says. "I think the ferocity with which we embrace work from home and protected it when it looked like it was going to be threatened speaks to how desperate families are to find every last minute because they need them." But when you throw in the difference between the workday and school day, the commute time makes a lot of work completely inaccessible to many Australians. "Once you factor in things like the time at which children can be dropped at school and what that's like for a young child in early primary years when they are dropped at school leads to whether that's actually even a solution for parents to be able to drop off when the school gates open," Dr Harrison Brennan says. "Factor in commute times to an office, and increasingly families needing to move further out in our major cities in Australia. "As soon as you get out into some of the kind of commuter suburbs, it makes actually commuting into a job in the city or somewhere else in a metropolitan city just not even a thing for families."

20 minutes per day For drop-off and pick-up. And that's being conservative. Read more Read more While distances are much greater in rural or regional areas, most (78 per cent) primary school-aged parents live within 2 kilometres of their school. That may be a 2-minute drive or a 15-minute walk. But if we're conservative and allow 10 minutes for each drop-off and pick-up, which realistically, doesn't also account for the time it takes to get everyone out of the house, settle the kids at school and get back, that's roughly 1.7 hours per week. Professor Hill says for workers who work a "typical" workday of 9am-5pm or 8am-6pm, the school pick-up is a real problem. "It's a hard stop, and it typically happens when you're kind of reaching peak productivity in your working day."

1 hour per week For extracurricular activities. Read more Read more It's hard to get the exact figures on how many activities children do and how much time parents spend attending them, but increasingly Australian families are feeling the pressure to enrol their kids in sports, arts, swimming and tutoring. The last Australian Bureau of Statistics survey into children's participation in cultural and leisure activities found 35 per cent of kids aged 5 to 14 did a cultural activity outside of school hours. About 60 per cent did an organised sport and spent about 5 hours a fortnight training or playing outside of school hours. Let's be conservative and allow 1 hour of the working week for dropping off and attending extracurricular activities, (even though it's likely to be more for most families). Often this involves working parents coming up with creative solutions like carpooling, working from the sidelines or logging back on when the children are in bed. Professor Hill says some parents feel penalised for accessing flexibility for this. "Just because they pick up their kids from daycare or from school or take them to netball practice, or to piano lessons, does not mean that they're any less committed as an employee and any less deserving of access to training opportunities or promotion opportunities."

24 days per year For school holidays. And that's if parents take all of their annual leave separately. Read more Read more The average Australian worker gets four weeks of annual leave, but there are 12 weeks of school holidays. Then there are at least four pupil-free or curriculum days to cover (in some states there are up to eight). Even if there are two parents at home who each have four weeks of annual leave and they choose to take all of their leave separately, which means no family holiday time, there's still a gap of more than four weeks. There are sometimes school holiday program options, but they can be costly. Dr Harrison Brennan says kids often need this time for downtime at home and with family and friends. "Many parents, they look to the school holidays and think, 'Oh, finally, this is going to be a chance to regroup.' "And then the realisation comes in that first year of school, 'Oh no, now we have to look at holiday care options', because even if you have four weeks of annual leave and two parents in a household, that's only going to cover about two-thirds of a child's annual school holidays." She says it's an outdated set-up we're dealing with. "It's just such a clear example of our models for the purposes of annual leave for workers and the purpose of school holidays for children being at complete odds with one another. "It's affecting kids, it's affecting families and extended families as well as grandparents being asked to do more. And sometimes that's possible, sometimes it's simply not."

At least 814 hours That's how much time parents have to find each year if both parents are working full-time and have primary school children. Read more Read more That overlap, when your job and your children need your attention, works out to be about 34 full days every year. And we know this is being conservative. Obviously it doesn't take into account the many variables in different family situations. It doesn't reflect families that have only one parent and/or children with additional needs. It's not counting the huge amount of unpaid work, cooking, cleaning, washing, planning, maintenance or day-to-day caregiving, that needs to be done for a family to run smoothly. It also doesn't factor in the assemblies, the medical appointments, the early pick-up days, the school events or homework. "The numbers are damning but they're not surprising," Georgie Dent says. "Those additional hours, they're so unseen until you're in the midst of it," Dr Harrison Brennan says. "Parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands," Dr Strazdins says.

Dr Strazdins says it's time to talk about the broken system.

"We've got lots of reasons why we do need to have this conversation," she says.

" If you're trying to find an extra 800 hours a year, well, what are you actually doing to do that? I mean, what actually are people trying to do if they're trying to find those extra hours? "

There is a lot of evidence to show that time pressure changes how people behave, Dr Strazdins says.

"They're rushing, they're feeling incredibly anxious, they're cutting back on other things that they really need to do.

"It's really a social problem to put this much pressure on citizens."

Professor Hill says society needs to recognise that intensive child care does not end when young kids start school.

"I think it's really good to name it and to shine a light on the quantum of hours that require some form of adult supervision, whether it's parents, whether it's grandparents, whether it's other community members."

Mums are in paid work more, but still carry larger portion of unpaid workload

Between 1990 and 2025, the proportion of two-parent families in which both partners worked rose from 55 per cent to 71-73 per cent, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

Over the past 20 years, the hours of paid work has grown for women.

This chart shows the hours worked when there is a child under 15 in the home, broken down by men and women.

Median hours of working men haven't changed much.

Across the past 20 years, they've sat at about 40 hours per week.

For quite some time, working hours of women hovered between 24 and 25 hours a week.

But since about 2016, those hours have been rising.

ABS data shows the median hours for mums is currently about 30 hours.

And that's the same whether they are in a two-parent or single-parent home.

But the data also shows historically those hours fluctuate a lot and continue to do so.

The dips in hours show that women's work has been more flexible to accommodate the school holidays.

All of the notable downward spikes in this chart appear to align with the four school holiday periods in summer, autumn, winter and spring.

The biggest drop shows a holiday period in 2012/2013 known as the "Angry Summer".

Catastrophic bushfires, extreme heat and devastating floods were simultaneously happening across the country, which may explain the dramatic dip in hours for both men and women employees at this time.

But it hasn't been the norm for both men's and women's hours to change during the holidays.

If we look at 2014 as an example, we can see that men's hours remained unchanged throughout the year, while women's hours zigzag during the school holiday periods.

However, that is changing.

In more recent years, men's hours have been fluctuating during these periods too.

If we fast-forward to 2024, men's hours reduce across the four holiday periods.

This may indicate that more dads are reducing hours to accommodate the school holiday juggle.

However the size of the dips indicate that women are still having their hours disrupted more dramatically.

Increasing financial pressures mean families often don't have a choice about whether or not both parents should work, or work more.

In homes where there is a couple and children aged 0-14 years, about 36 per cent have both parents working full-time.

The way society is built has not kept up with the reality of modern family life, Georgie Dent says.

" There are more parents than ever in paid work, not as a lifestyle choice, but out of necessity, yet so many of our systems, from schools to workplaces to paid parental leave and child care, still reflect an outdated assumption that there's a parent at home to readily absorb the care and domestic load of raising a family. "

And not only that, the economy wants women to work more.

Australian women work part-time at higher rates than many other advanced economies.

In an economic roundtable a year ago, economists highlighted that women were an untapped resource for our nation's productivity.

"We've got women working shorter hours, doing the rest, helping men work the long hours and making the money … but it's not in the country's interests and it's certainly not equal," Dr Strazdins says.

This is reflected in the amount of unpaid work mums do, compared to dads.

An ABS survey reveals mothers do more than 2 hours of extra unpaid work and have 24 minutes less leisure time each day than fathers.

Georgie Dent says our economy relies on the unpaid work of women.

" We've built an economy and society that runs on the invisible labour of parents, particularly mums, and called it a 'work-life balance problem' instead of a policy failure. "

A flood of comments in a recent ABC social media post highlighted that many mums felt like they weren't juggling, they were struggling.



"Working hours and school hours do not make sense … this is structural inequality that guarantees failings for all parents, but especially mums. We've lost before we even walk out the front door." - @lauren_affairs_and_trade



Another commenter said: "We're not juggling, we're sacrificing our own mental, physical and emotional health to meet the structures of a system designed for a different time." - @otto.von.gram

What society needs to do to keep up

The majority of our workforce are 'worker-carers' — people who have responsibilities at both work and home.

Experts say there is no silver-bullet solution to overhaul the system, but propose a suite of changes to better support modern families.

Flexible workplaces But it needs to be for both men and women. Read more Read more This can come in many different forms, says Rowena Ditzell, who specialises in the future of work. "People are talking about working from home and that's certainly a really common way of flexible working, but there's many other ways, whether it's flexible start and finish times, which can really help parents with school-aged children, whether it's term hours, you know, things like that can make a real difference for working parents." A four-day work week is one possible solution to a more flexible work environment, Dr Ditzell says. "Certainly in my research I have spoken to women who have told me that because they have been able to do a relatively important role, but been able to do it in four days, they wouldn't have been able to access that role beforehand. "Rather than thinking to be successful or to be taking your career seriously, you need to be in the office five days a week, it's about: to be successful you need to be delivering your outcomes." Dr Ditzell says while more Australians are able to access workplace flexibility, it needs to come without the worry of being overlooked for pay increases or promotions. "We still see what we call either flexibility stigma or flexibility bias and that is the situation where people who use flexibility actually feel that they are disadvantaged as a result of that and they feel that they are judged differently." Experts say for the gender pay gap to shrink and the glass ceiling to break, more men need to take up the flexibility too and employers need to recognise that mums and dads have equal responsibility for children. Professor Hill says research suggests men can suffer from flexibility stigma in more extreme ways than women. "If flexible work arrangements are not taken up by men as well, then they risk becoming just another reason for women to continue doing a disproportionate amount of unpaid care work," she says. Dr Strazdins says flexibility should no longer be seen as a nice to have under Australian Work Health and Safety laws. "There's legislation now, and it's called psychosocial hazards … parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands." She also argues it's time to crack down on working hours beyond the mandated 38-hour work week. "While we allow long-hour jobs to be so well incentivised and earned, households have to make a really tough choice: who earns the big bucks and works the long hours and then who does the rest?"

Better after-school care That's affordable and in the same place as the school. Read more Read more Kate Harrison Brennan says reliable after-school care, ideally in the same location the child goes to school, is the backbone to stable employment. "Quality, affordable care is crucial, particularly for workers who aren't able to be flexible with their working hours."

Extra parental leave And not just for parents with babies. Read more Read more This could look like extra leave for parents of young children, beyond when they're babies, to give families more time together. "I think this mismatch between the hours that we are at work and the hours that they are at school really demands that we think in new ways around paid leave away from work in order to provide those supports," Professor Hill says. "We've always thought about 'paid parental leave' as being something only relevant to the first year of a child's life, but there are countries where there's an expectation that parents have access to paid leave throughout the early years of a child's schooling as well." In Sweden parents get 480 days of paid parental leave per child, shared between the parents. That can be banked and used flexibly throughout their childhood.

Capped hours To stop incentivising one parent. Read more Read more Dr Strazdins says legislating against excessive work hours can level the playing field and reduce the gender pay gap. "There's a review of the National Employment Standards right now. I would say there's very few employment standards which are so routinely ignored as the work hours per week. "I'm trying to get people to see that it's really not right for workplaces to expect people to work these excessive hours – even if they reward them for it."

More men taking on mental load To balance the unpaid workload. Read more Read more Men need to step up and do more of the unpaid work, and society needs to make that more possible, Professor Hill says. "It's a big task. It's mostly invisible. It's squeezed in around everything else. It creates huge cognitive, emotional and logistical pressure that is primarily borne by mothers and grandmothers, and we need community and workplace supports that recognise that and allow it to be distributed more equally between all caregivers. "Importantly, in offering and providing that flexibility, it's really critical that employers don't penalise dads for contributing to the unpaid care load."

We can’t expect families to keep patching over the gaps, Georgie Dent says.

" We're effectively asking parents to run a marathon in shoes designed for someone else and then wondering why they're not keeping up. "

She says sytems that don't match modern-day realities are not only leaving parents scrambling, but they're failing children.

And perhaps, one of the biggest changes required is an attitude one.

“Supporting parents isn’t a concession to adult convenience: it’s one of the most powerful things we can do for the next generation," Ms Dent says.

“When we invest in parents, we invest in children."

title: Why the Canberra community is up in arms over an abandoned water park
text:
Tell us about your experience.

If you grew up in Canberra, you might have fond memories of the capital's only outdoor water park, Big Splash.

It had been a public swimming pool in Macquarie in Canberra's north before it was bought by a family in the 90s and transformed into an attraction of slides.

That family sold up, and for the past couple of years the water park has been an increasingly dilapidated husk of its former self.

The state of the park, and several broken promises over its unrealised reopening, have caused frustration.

And anyone still hoping the water park will feature in their summer plans is likely to be left high and dry.

Big Splash water park's pool is disused and green. (ABC News)

Why isn't the government taking over?

The community has been frustrated by the lack of ACT government enforcement in relation to the site.

The government has been asked several times why it does not purchase, restore and publicly run the park.

It has never ruled that out, but said its strong preference was for the park to remain privately operated.

ACT government regulator Access Canberra has the capacity to issue a controlled activity order, which carries a penalty of up to $48,600, or to terminate the lease of the land completely.

So far, the government has refused to be drawn on exactly what it would take to enact those processes.

Who owns Big Splash water park?

The original Big Splash operators ran the park for decades before the lease was sold during the pandemic for a reported $7.5 million.

Like much of the capital, Big Splash is on a 99-year crown lease, which was last renewed 20 years ago.

The lease conditions for the 13,000-square-metre parcel of land stipulate that it must house either an aquatic facility, an indoor sports facility, or an unlicensed family restaurant.

The lessee, Translink Management Group, signed the contract in 2021, with the clauses unchanged.

Why hasn't Big Splash reopened?

After closing in 2024, the site was slated to reopen in November 2025, but the lessee did not deliver and blamed rising repair costs.

That same month, the ACT government confirmed the lessee had ambitions for the site to be rezoned for residential use, but that desire was shot down by the government, which said it had no plans for the area to be used for anything but its recreational purpose.

In April this year, Access Canberra decided against following through on a threat to terminate the lease, saying it was satisfied the owners had made moves to reopen the facility's 50-metre pool before next summer.

Have there been any offers to buy the park?

Big Splash water park is listed as for sale. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

In June this year, the water park was put up for sale.

At the time, work to fix the main pool and ticketing facilities was set to continue, but recent images of the property tell a different story.

The ABC has been told no acceptable offer was received during the expressions of interest process and the property remains available for purchase.

Financiers have taken over decision-making

The 50-metre pool remains covered in vandalism. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Labor MLA for Ginninderra Tara Cheyne recently confirmed the person behind Translink Management Group was no longer calling the shots.

"I've met with these people now who have taken over and they are different to the person who effectively let Big Splash go into disrepair," Ms Cheyne said.

"They are the people who lent the money to him ... basically a small financing business running out of Sydney."

She described the group as "genuine".

Is a food van next for the site?

On Wednesday, the ACT government said it feared its latest deadline for the pool to reopen would not be met.

And ACT Planning Minister Chris Steel announced a "comprehensive options analysis", which would ask for public feedback.

But that solution was criticised by the ACT Greens, who insisted it was already clear the community wanted a water park.

Just a day later, on Thursday, the owners of Big Splash announced they would comply with their lease requirements by operating an unlicensed family restaurant at the site by November.

Big Splash Waterpark is not far from Belconnen's central shops. (Supplied: Colliers)

Head of Access Canberra Josh Rynehart confirmed a temporary way to do that could be to put a food van on the site.

What's next?

There are two possible outcomes as November approaches:

The first is that a food outlet pops up and authorities are temporarily satisfied. Though, many in the community will likely be unhappy, including the Save Big Splash group.

The second is that the deadline comes and goes with inaction, leading to renewed questions over enforcement.

There is a third, wildcard option, which could see the property sold. But that would not guarantee the buyer would be interested in restoring the water park.

The ABC has been told a builder has been engaged, with a deposit paid, in a bid to house a restaurant on the site by November.

title: New Lego exhibition shows creative result of 'not following instructions'
text:
Tell us about your experience.

It's the year 2130, humans have left Earth and Lego minifigures have moved into the belongings we've left behind.

At least that's how friends Jackson Harvey and Alex Towler imagined the future, while they spent years creating a whimsical, wonder-filled world for their exhibition RELICS: A New World Rises.

"The characters of Relics live in a world that's set in the not-too-distant future … where humans have left the planet for reasons that are left vague. But they have built new communities inside all the old objects and junk that we've left behind," Harvey explains.

A bustling Lego society housed inside a Volkswagen beetle boot. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Across more than 15 large-scale installations at the Canberra Museum and Gallery, tiny communities have moved into the wreckage humanity left behind.

A fridge has become a cryogenic wellness resort, a grandfather clock has been reverse-engineered by a band of inventors into a time machine, a claw machine has become a futuristic space port.

"Lego has become [the] majority of our lives. It's lots of fun though — it changes the way we've looked at the world," Towler says.

Lego people mingle at a resort, in a world abandoned by humans. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

"We just like looking at cool stuff and figuring out what little plastic people will do with them," he says.

Vintage classics house intricate worlds

The pair created this new civilisation from old stuff.

"This exhibition was built on a majority of salvaged parts. It's mostly second-hand Lego," Towler says.

The pair blended relics with Lego to invoke nostalgia for viewers. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Some of the objects were harder to find than others, the pair say. And all the detail that surrounds the larger objects help to build the story and the world.

"We've got a lot of really unique objects in the exhibition — some of them are really hard to find," Harvey says.

" My personal favourite is the 76-year-old jukebox, the antique Wurlitzer from the 40s. "

Immersive art

Harvey and Towler say there are many stories woven into the millions of small pieces and 2,500 minifigures making up the exhibition.

Harvey and Towler sourced an old jukebox for one installation. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

"Lego is only a small part of this exhibition," Towler says.

"There's a lot to see. There's the stories, there's the nostalgia of the objects, there's the scavenger hunt to help explore the detail. There's something for everybody in this exhibition."

They say the longer you look at it, the more you'll uncover.

"There's lots of little Easter eggs and hidden stories that you can only find if you look around a corner and down a hallway or behind a shelf," Harvey says.

They've built it. Now you can come

"This exhibition is at its core about not following instructions, doing something differently," Towler says.

Harvey and Towler want to encourage people to think outside 'normal' ways of doing things. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"Lego pieces aren't meant to fit in the front of a VW Beetle, but if you have a V-Dub and you have Lego and you squish them together, you can figure it out. That's the message."

The exhibition is designed to appeal equally to serious enthusiasts, families and anyone who's never clicked a little plastic brick in their life.

RELICS: A New World Rises is a ticketed exhibition on at the Canberra Museum and Gallery until January 31, 2027.

title: How knitting and crochet can be 'deceptively good' for the brain
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Will Seager taught himself to knit nine years ago. Now, it's something he does every day.

"I'm naturally a little bit of an anxious person so for me it's really nice to let go of any other worries or things that I need to be thinking about and focus entirely on my knitting," Mr Seager said.

Will Seager says knitting is both relaxing and challenging. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"I do it also because it's very intellectually stimulating for me … I like to choose patterns which are technically quite demanding and quite difficult."

Neuroscientist Sarah McKay said crafts such as knitting and crochet were "deceptively good for the brain".

"It's like this ideal mix of repetition plus cognitive challenge," Dr McKay said.

Will Seager says he likes to continually challenge himself by seeking out more complex patterns. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"You have to remember where you're up to, you have to problem solve, you have to make decisions, you're constantly challenging yourself if you're doing more and more complicated patterns.

"But at the same time, it's challenging but it's low stakes … which I think might be one of the best kinds [of cognitive challenge] we can have."

Dr McKay said craft activities could help with attention.

"What they're doing is they're almost training us to pay attention to something for quite a long time," she said.

Will Seager enjoys knitting socks. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Researchers have also studied how useful craft activities could be for mood regulation and stress reduction.

"We're mastering a skill, we're getting better at that and we're kind of just doing the task for the sake of doing the task … it's quite a simple form of mastery and there's something really soothing and good for our mood about that," Dr McKay said.

Mr Seager is constantly looking for new ways to challenge himself as a knitter.

"I like to choose patterns that enable me to learn new skills … Most recently I've got into a type of [ribbed] knitting called brioche knitting," he said.

" It took me a long time to get the hang of it … [but] after a little while you settle into the rhythm and your fingers and hands do the work without you having to think too much about it. "

Brioche knitting is a technique Will Seager has recently become interested in. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Mr Seager likes to knit alone so he can focus.

But, for others, craft is a way to connect with people.

Looking after each other through craft

Once a week in Hobart's northern suburbs, the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group meets. Its members mostly knit and crochet items to donate to local charities.

"Some of the ladies [who come], this is their only outing apart from the supermarket," said Carolee Marino, who started the group in 2011.

"It's all about looking after each other … we all help each other."

Carolee Marino started the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group in 2011. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

One of the group's newest members is Gill Shilling.

"It's awesome. I've met all these amazing ladies with interesting stories," Ms Shilling said.

"But the fact that we're actually making things to give to people in the community who are in need, that's really important to me."

Gill Shilling (left) says she enjoys the social aspect of the group, as well as contributing to charity. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Another relatively new group member, Irina Bridges, learnt to knit after moving to Australia from Russia seven years ago.

She said she was looking to share her love of knitting with others.

"I dreamt to knit my whole life, but I couldn't because when I was a kid in Soviet Union all stores were empty without yarn," Ms Bridges said.

"I enjoy our group and showing off what I [have] knitted."

Irina Bridges enjoys sharing her love of knitting with others. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Miriam Ritchie has been part of the group for about two years.

"This is it — this is my social — and I get pretty lonely, so I can't wait to get here," she said.

Miriam Ritchie (right) looks forward to catching up with the other members of the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Norma Kelaart joined the group after moving to Tasmania in 2024.

"I needed some company of other women to chat with and relax with and have a joke and a laugh," she said.

One part of a broader brain health plan

Dr McKay said that while there was not enough evidence to prove that activities such as knitting and crochet helped prevent dementia, many of the studies were observational and self-reported, not randomised clinical trials that look specifically at dementia risk.

The magical healing power of crochet The steady click of needles and hooks on couches around Australia tells us that knitters have been onto the very real therapeutic benefits of crochet for a long time.

She said the many clear benefits meant craft activities could be an important part of a broader lifestyle brain health program.

"Alongside exercise and diet and sleep and stress reduction … [and] taking care of your cardiovascular health, your metabolic health — all of the things that we know are good for our mental health in the short term and our brain health long term — this can sit really nicely and neatly in there," she said.

"We know that social connections are a really important part of long-term brain health, [and] we know that having purpose and meaning in life are a really important part of brain health, so it can fulfil those requirements in a really lovely, non-digital way."

title: Fishy freight lands in Tasmania ahead of Bass Strait trial
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Placed in oxygenated bags then packed into insulated boxes, 15,000 juvenile kingfish have made the 3,000-kilometre journey from Fremantle to Hobart.

The arrival of the tiny fish, known as fingerlings, marks the next stage of aquaculture trial underway in Bass Strait, 12 kilometres off the coast of Burnie.

The packages travelled in two specialist air-freight shipments, packed in oxygenated bags sealed inside insulated polyboxes. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Blue Economy CRC says the cargo arrived safely. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Researcher and kingfish impact lead for the company running the trial, Blue Economy CRC (Cooperative Research Centre), Maxi Canepa, said the journey was "an interesting exercise".

"We didn't have mortalities. They are fantastic. They looked very healthy on arrival," he said.

"These fish grow really fast. That's why it's a very nice species for aquaculture."

The kingfish will grow to be around four kilograms when mature. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

The fingerlings will grow on land at the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) in Taroona for three months until they weigh between 100 and 150 grams.

The not-so-tiny fish will then be transported to the trial site, where they will be acclimatised to the water and released into a sea pen where they are expected to grow to 4 kilograms before being harvested.

The kingfish will be held in tanks at the University of Tasmania's IMAS aquaculture research facility at Taroona for about three months. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Dr Canepa said it would be the first time kingfish are farmed offshore in Australia.

"It's a site that is going to offer some challenges but also opportunities," he said.

Blue Economy CRC says the fish pen infrastructure "stood up to the high-energy conditions of Bass Strait". (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

How will fish fare in 'wild' Bass Strait?

The three-year research trial, dubbed the Blue Economy Zone (BEZ), is the country's first aquaculture trial in Commonwealth waters, led by independent not-for-profit Blue Economy CRC.

The company is part of the federal government's CRC program, which supports industry-led collaborations between industry, researchers and the community.

The project aims to trial the viability of multi-species offshore aquaculture in Commonwealth waters.

In 2028 the site will be decommissioned; and any commercial operation will then be a question for aquaculture companies and will require government approvals.

Blue Economy CRC says the kingfish "are gradually acclimatised to the waters before being released into the research sea pen" in Bass Strait. (Supplied: Blue Economy CRC)

Three months after pens were established in 2025, 15,000 Atlantic salmon were introduced. Last week, the fish were harvested.

Blue Economy CRC chief executive Angela Williamson says the salmon "performed really well" in the notoriously rough waters of Bass Strait.

"They grew above the predicted modelled weight. Unlike within the state waters, they did not need to be bathed. We did experience regular mortalities across that time period," she said.

"All our information was put on our website on a dashboard. We know transparency is a really important component of this trial and (the public) understanding and trusting the process," she said.

Ms Williamson said infrastructure had also held up against the "wild and windy" conditions.

"We've had to really make sure that our mooring grid, our nets and our floating equipment meet those standards, not just of government, but also of keeping the fish safe, keeping people who are operating safe, and ensuring that marine debris is eliminated as much as possible."

According to the project's dashboard, the BEZ has recorded 13 pieces of marine debris and eight "wildlife interactions".

The kingfish will be transferred into large tanks aboard a vessel for the 12.5-kilometre journey into Bass Strait. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Opposition to trial in north-west

A public meeting hosted by Blue Economy CRC was held when the project at the start of the trial last year, with attendees opposed to the trial expressing concerns about environmental impacts.

Opponents attended a public forum on the fish farming trial in May, 2025. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Tasmanian independent Braddon MP Craig Garland is staunchly opposed to the trial.

"We never wanted any salmon or any finfish aquaculture in our waterways," he said.

"One in five people are coming here for the tourism experience. They're not coming to see a flow-through hatch with algae growing downstream. They're not coming to see 20,000 ton of dead fish rotting and floating around the place."

Spike in dolphin deaths prompts questioning Tasmanian regulators question major salmon farm operator Huon Aquaculture about the effectiveness of its "predator" nets after a spate of dolphin deaths.

From January to April 2025, a bacterial disease known as Piscirickettsia salmonis caused the mass deaths of salmon in pens in south-east Tasmanian waters.

Data reported to the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) showed almost 15,000 tonnes of dead salmon during that period went to waste facilities.

Ms Williamson said there are a "variety of perspectives" on aquaculture across coastal communities.

"I think the debate about aquaculture more broadly across Australia is a strong debate," she said.

"At the end of the day, what we're looking to do is learn from all of those and provide for a regulatory environment, a policy environment that makes sense for Commonwealth waters, which are further offshore."

The company says the research is "about what greater sovereign seafood production could look like and the role our oceans can play in Australia's food and nutrition security". (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Trial infrastructure to be decommissioned in 2028

How many salmon farms are there in Tasmania — and who owns them? Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them.

After the kingfish are harvested in May 2028, the site will be decommissioned and the research findings will inform future governance of aquaculture in government waters.

Harvested salmon, kingfish and seaweed products are allowed to be sold under the project's permit arrangement, with profits fed back into the CRC program to offset research costs.

"There'll be a wealth of information and knowledge available for industry and government to make decisions on what's next and whether that is unlocking Commonwealth waters right around Australia, what that looks like, how that will be done," Ms Williamson said.

title: 'Hell on earth' for owners of units of collapsed developer at heart of ICAC
text:
When Michael Jones bought his first home in 2017, his wife was pregnant with their first child.

The two-bedroom apartment at Toplace's Vicinity complex in Sydney was meant to be their "nest egg", a place to build memories for the young family.

Nine years and two more children later, his family has long outgrown the apartment.

But major structural defects in the complex have left them financially trapped.

Mr Jones says his dreams and aspirations have been put off. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"We certainly didn't imagine that there would be three children stacked up in bunks in the same room," the 40-year-old said.

"It certainly puts off the dreams and aspirations that you would have when you're my age … I would have expected by now that I would have a house that fits the amount of people that we have."

Mr Jones is one of thousands of Toplace apartment owners left to pick up the pieces of the company's collapse amid a dramatic inquiry before the NSW Independent Corruption Against Corruption (ICAC).

At the heart of it all is Toplace founder, Jean Nassif, who has remained defiant as he continues to defend the crumbled property empire he built.

Huge losses and debts

At Vicinity, temporary steel props have been supporting parts of the building since 2022, after engineers raised concerns about key structural beams.

Owners have faced repair estimates running into the millions, with one structural issue alone estimated at $11 million.

Mr Jones projects he has spent an additional $150,000 on strata costs and repairs since 2017.

He said the apartments that once sold for as much as $800,000 may now be worth as little as $250,000 to $380,000.

Owners at the Vicinity apartment complex have been bearing the brunt, and costs, of structural defects. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

It has meant there is little escape for the owners.

Many are struggling to refinance, cannot sell without suffering huge losses, and are carrying debts on homes they cannot easily leave.

Some neighbours have taken on extra jobs.

"The irony of having the last name Jones and not even being able to 'keep up with the Joneses' is not lost on me," he said.

'No-one can make me shut up!'

During Mr Nassif's highly-anticipated appearance at the ICAC this week, where he appeared twice, his rage was palpable.

Appearing via video call from his bedroom in Beirut, he spent several hours protesting his innocence, ranting and lashing out.

At one point, Assistant Commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC intervened, prompting another tirade from Mr Nassif.

Mr Nassif spent several hours during his testimony over two days protesting his innocence and lashing out. (ABC News)

Mr Gleeson: "The purpose of this inquiry is to get to the truth of certain allegations. It's not for you to attack other people. "I'd like you to just pause, no, no. Please listen to me. I've listened to you." Mr Nassif: "No. No. No. No. No. No. No-one can make me shut up."

The 58-year-old, who is wanted by NSW Police on fraud charges, denied he was hiding from Australian authorities in Lebanon, claiming he has not returned because he has faced multiple death threats.

He told the inquiry he was not corrupt, and blamed former Liberal minister David Elliott and former state building commissioner David Chandler for the demise of Toplace.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC put to Mr Nassif: "They [Mr Chandler and Mr Elliott] alleged that there were structural defects with Toplace projects, is that right?" "They alleged that. That's not true," Mr Nassif said.

Mr Nassif has been accused of trying to damage Mr Elliott's career and have Mr Chandler removed as the commissioner to stop him investigating Mr Nassif's developments.

Both Mr Elliott and Mr Chandler are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Mr Nassif has blamed Mr Elliott (left) and Mr Chandler for the demise of Toplace. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow, Abubakr Sajid)

'Death of their dream home'

Mr Chandler found multiple defects in several Toplace buildings and used his appearance earlier in the inquiry to point to the "real victims": the owners and occupiers.

The head of the residential strata body, Owners Corporation Network, Karen Stiles, told the ABC the damage could not be measured in dollars alone.

"It was hell on earth for the owners. Tenants too were subjected to disruptions, poor living conditions, noise, and stress," Ms Stiles said.

Ms Stiles recalled residents being forced out of their homes with little warning, sometimes unable to retrieve pets of belongings.

Ms Stiles says it has been "hell on earth" for owners. (ABC News: Amy Greenbank)

She said one elderly couple built a makeshift dam in their lounge room to keep floodwater out, while another woman had to be rescued after her apartment door jammed with subsidence.

"I could say that serious defects impacted owners physically, financially, and emotionally. But that's just words," she said.

" The full picture is miscarriages, broken marriages, serious health impacts. "

Ms Stiles added that many owners were left grieving the "death of their dream home".

"While ICAC investigates corruption, exposing small people playing silly games, let's give a thought to the thousands of victims of the cavalier chess moves played with their lives," she said.

'Unedifying' evidence at ICAC

Former ICAC assistant commissioner and chair of the Centre for Public Integrity, Anthony Whealy KC, said the inquiry has "shone a very unedifying light" on activities between the state's Liberal Party, lobbyists, and developers like Mr Nassif.

While Mr Whealy believes the commission has been well-represented by counsel assisting, he said proving that it goes beyond the ugly side of politics will be difficult.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

"Their task now will be to pull all that evidence together and to put a compelling portrait to say, if this is to be their submission, this isn't just a matter of factional warfare or quarrelling," Mr Whealy said.

"They'll have to amount this argument that there are deliberate attempts on the part of all of the key personnel, together with Nassif, to actually corrupt the political process."

For owners like Mr Jones, he hopes the public inquiry offers accountability, but worries there may be little consequence for those responsible.

"My fear is that this is a toothless beast that will end up wagging the finger at a few people," Mr Jones said.

"It should be a 'Come to Jesus' moment where we see real change happen in a time where we need to go through a construction boom."

title: An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech
text:

NationalVictoriaLocal council An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech Lachlan Abbott September 19, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A self-styled council watchdog has won an appeal against an intervention order granted to an inner-eastern Melbourne mayor after a judge ruled his social media posts, including one depicting her as Miss Piggy, were protected political speech. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston hailed the County Court judgment released late on Friday as a win for democratic scrutiny of elected officials, as it overturned the court order Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr was granted last year. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston (left) and Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr. Simon Schluter, Luis Enrique Ascui Magistrate Michelle Hodgson previously found “the gendered and personal undertones” of Hurlston’s posts and text messages to Sehr in recent years “crossed the line from fair commentary into targeted ridicule” that was intended to cause mental harm. But County Court judge Julie Clayton disagreed and on Friday threw out the personal safety intervention order against Hurlston.

Advertisement

Clayton found the magistrate’s interpretation of political commentary protected under Victorian law was too narrow and Hurlston’s posts were primarily motivated by concern about the City of Stonnington’s governance. Related Article CBD Council activist apologises – twice – after accusing councillor of sexual harassment “The personal integrity of politicians, quite apart from their policy positions, is a legitimate subject for news and current affairs,” Clayton wrote. On Saturday, Hurlston criticised Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson for claiming the magistrate’s initial ruling was a “landmark court decision” before it was overturned. “The council’s triumphal public statement now stands as a monument to poor judgment,” Hurlston said.

Advertisement

“This case should concern every journalist, activist, ratepayer and community watchdog. If robust criticism of public officials can be repackaged as a personal safety matter, democratic scrutiny itself is placed at risk.” Sehr compiled an almost 500-page dossier of posts from Hurlston’s Stonnington Council Watch Facebook page and other messages that she said had escalated to personal harassment. The judge accepted Sehr (pictured) felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but found her fear wasn’t the same as a fear for her safety. Ruby Alexander Clayton said Hurlston was “an enormous nuisance” to Sehr and some of the posts were hurtful, including one that accused the mayor of using her mother’s death to avoid questions. She accepted the mayor felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but added: “That sort of fear, however, is not the same as a fear for one’s safety.”

Advertisement

The judge ultimately found Hurlston’s posts were published without malicious intent and thus an intervention order could not be made. The previous order restricted Hurlston’s online commentary towards Sehr and barred him from coming within two metres of her. “Mr Hurlston may not abide by a journalistic code of conduct in relation to fair and balanced commentary,” Clayton said. “This does not mean he is not entitled to the protection afforded by [the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act].” She added: “It is permissible for Mr Hurlston to publish, filled with ill-will, animosity, spite and hostility if the actuating motive for the publication is not improper.” Clayton said the images Hurlston posted of Miss Piggy and a cartoon of a stereotypical housewife could be seen as demeaning or derogatory towards Sehr.

Advertisement

Hurlston said the Miss Piggy image referred to Sehr as a “muppet” as it was a common derogatory term in politics, and it was not intended to attack her appearance. Related Article City life Mega merger not the answer to funding shortfall, councils say The judge acknowledged Sehr felt humiliated, but was not persuaded the image was primarily motived by something other than Hurlston’s political opinion that the mayor was “not up to the job”. The judge also said the housewife cartoon was not substantially different from thousands of other political caricatures. “Women in public life generally, and politics in particular are often unfairly targeted in relation to their appearance,” Clayton wrote.

“While one might bemoan this sorry state of affairs it is not a state of affairs that the act was intended to address.” Sehr told The Age she was awaiting further legal advice after Friday’s decision. title: International students flock to Australian universities. Here is what they study

NationalUniversity International students flock to Australian universities. Here is what they study Siena Fagan September 19, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luis Guzman grew up with Australia in his sights. After watching the film Kangaroo Jack as a six-year-old in Guatemala, he told his mother the country would one day be his home. At 18 he came down under to travel. At 28 he enrolled in a master’s degree in event management at the UTS Business School. Luis Guzman moved to Sydney from Guatamala to study. “The quality of life, the opportunities that I can have here … I think it’s really nice.” Wolter Peeters Now in his final semester, Guzman has high hopes for the future. He dreams of working in Formula 1 racing, and meanwhile is developing his entrepreneurship skills. He hopes to stay in Australia after graduating. The opportunities, he says, are unparallelled.

Advertisement

“I know that in Australia, if I work hard and I put effort in, I can achieve more.” Related Article Updated

Immigration Labor’s tough new migration rules target backpackers, foreign students and overstayers Guzman is one of hundreds of thousands of international students who come to Australian universities to pursue their dreams. Since 2021, international student enrolments at Australian universities increased by 46.2 per cent – from 314,619 to 460,090. Those numbers have been a primary target of the federal government’s plans, revealed on Thursday, to curb net migration from about 300,000 to 225,000 next year. It aims to curb the number of international students by targeting visa hopping and by reducing the influx of family members.

Advertisement

The most popular broad field of study for international students enrolled in Australian universities was management and commerce, accounting for 120,136 enrolments in 2026. Information technology ranked second, followed by society and culture. The most studied management and commerce disciplines were business and management (61,222 enrolments), followed by accounting (14,566 enrolments). Speaking before the migration changes were unveiled, International Education Association of Australia chief executive Phil Honeywood said those degrees had broad appeal to international neighbours, offering in-demand skills taught in a native English setting. “The overwhelming number of overseas students doing such courses come from family businesses where the parents would like their child to learn business practices in a native English-speaking country, and … go home to run the family business or to start in a larger corporation.”

Advertisement

Honeywood said on Thursday the reforms were “really a mixed bag” for international students but the changes were unlikely to impact the types of degrees that were most popular. Related Article Exclusive

University From Concord to the country: The student search for greener pastures in an AI world Guzman, who hopes to remain in Australia after his degree, says the variety of skills taught in business degrees made them desirable for domestic and international students. “People just want to gain … skills for management and skills for HR and skills for marketing,” he says. “You have more options whenever you’re looking for a job.” Guzman understood the need for the government to balance immigration with domestic matters but he was worried such reforms would affect perceptions of international students.

Advertisement

“If I talk with my friends who are international students, I think they are going to feel anxious about their futures,” he said. While management and commerce has maintained its position as the most-studied field by international students over the past five years, its contribution to enrolments dropped by 21.5 per cent. Honeywood says this coincides with the removal of finance and accounting from the Australian government’s skills-in-demand list. He warns that maintaining international access to these degrees is key to Australia’s soft power diplomacy in the region, as many neighbouring countries have relied on Australia for its educational experts for decades. There has also been an uptick in international enrolments in other fields.

Advertisement

In the past five years, enrolments in broad education degrees shot up 297.7 per cent – from 12,026 students in 2021 to 47,824 in 2026. title: Five years, millions of dollars: The battle to fix a defective Sydney building
text:

When Andrew and Lisa Cook moved into their new apartment in Baulkham Hills on December 12, 2020, they thought they were getting the dream: a modern unit, a sprawling balcony with views of the city skyline and access to shops at the base of their building. Just 23 days later, the dream became a nightmare: the company that developed the building collapsed. Ten months after that, the state’s building regulator identified serious defects in the development, including one that was labelled a “hazard to human life”. The Cooks were shocked. They didn’t know who would be responsible for fixing the defects, and what it meant for their new home. “[We were] a bit scared because they didn’t know what was going to happen at the time,” Lisa said. Andrew and Lisa Cook on their balcony, which is still being repaired. Jessica Hromas Known then as the Modena, the four-tower project was developed by Hills Shoppingtown Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of Dyldam Group – once one of NSW’s biggest apartment builders before it collapsed with debts of half a billion dollars. There were 230 apartments and plans for a retail precinct in a project designed to combine luxury and comfort. When the receivers for the development and the building regulator visited the site, they found it was far from that vision. In addition to non-compliant waterproofing, an awning in danger of collapse, balconies without water overflows, the glass elevator – designed as a key feature for the project – had already rusted and was leaning slightly.

Advertisement

For five years, the Cooks and a handful of other residents have lived in a construction zone as millions of dollars were funnelled into rectifying defects. The scale of the work is so significant that the Cooks have lived in another unit since January while work on their own apartment continues. “There’s been a lot of noise for quite a few years, so that’s sort of a bad thing, but I keep thinking they’re doing it, they’re fixing it, it’s not costing us any money,” Andrew said. The Baulkham Hills building, formerly known as the Modena. Jessica Hromas. The stairs to the lower lever remain fenced-off while work continues. Jessica Hromas “We’re one of the fortunate buildings in Sydney.” Buying a home with defects is not an uncommon experience in NSW. Building Commission NSW ordered major developer Bathla Group, which entered voluntary administration last month, to fix serious defects in two of its developments. It’s left those who purchased off the plan uncertain if they would ever move in. So when developers collapse owing millions of dollars, how do you fix a defective building?

Advertisement

The $70 million fix When McGrathNicol was appointed the receiver of the Modena development in 2021, partner Jason Ireland said they were told the project was 95 per cent complete. But what was anticipated to be a quick fix soon became a mammoth project that would take years and $70 million to rectify defects – bringing the total cost of completing the development to $185 million. Ireland describes the project as being a bit like an onion, “in that when you peeled back [layers], you found more problems that made you cry,” he said. More than 60 defects were found throughout the four buildings. McGrathNicol’s Jason Ireland said it has cost $70 million dollars to fix the defects left behind by the original builder. Jessica Hromas Fixing the overflow holes in balconies was considered a simple job. Then the tiles began to be removed, and a new problem appeared: No one could identify what waterproofing material had been used. Ireland said it was clear it was a non-compliant product. “We eventually got to the conclusion that the only way to actually get the sign-off in the end was to rip up the balconies, replace all of the waterproofing, and replace all of the tiling, which is a lot because there’s over 200 apartments,” he said. Through it all, the four buildings have been partially occupied. In a Tetris-like process, residents had to be moved from their apartments to another in the development to allow for each to be rectified in turn.

Advertisement

When the Herald visited last month, work was continuing. The elevator had been replaced, the stairs to the lower level remained fenced off and some balconies – including the Cooks’ – were still under repair. The new elevator, which the replaced the original, rusted one. Jessica Hromas Ireland said there is light at the end of the tunnel, with 90 per cent of the defects fixed. Building Commission NSW lifted its building work rectification and prohibition order for the development, which has been rebranded as “Alfresco Quarter”. An interim occupation certificate remains in place. In May, the commission accepted a voluntary undertaking from McGrathNicol, which will provide additional independent oversight of the development. About 50 per cent of the apartments have now been sold, and the empty retail precinct has been acquired by property services provider Mintus. The lower level will have a gym, and cafés and restaurants are planned for the upper level. Work will be completed next year. An artist’s impression of what the cafe at the Baulkham Hills development would look like. Alfresco Quarter Ireland said: “The silver lining to the cloud is that if you buy a property in this building, you know it’s been through the highest of verification standards by the building commissioner’s team. They have been through it with a fine tooth comb.

Advertisement

“Some of the people [living] here have been to hell and back, but importantly, back.” The lucky ones Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it staves off liquidation It’s been a difficult, drawn-out process for the Cooks, but they’ve remained positive and hope to move back into their own apartment before the end of the year. “This is our forever home,” Andrew said. “And the tiles they put down are much nicer than the old ones.” Despite the stress it’s caused, the Cooks consider themselves lucky; unlike many other owners living in buildings with defects built by collapsed developers, the family didn’t have to fund the repairs. At the Vicinity complex in Canterbury, owners are still picking up the tab after major structural defects were discovered in parts of the 276-apartment complex, which was built by collapsed developer Toplace.
