title: Fed up with taxes, Aussies are following Adrian Portelli to Dubai. The ATO is watching
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaDubai Fed up with taxes, Aussies are following Adrian Portelli to Dubai. The ATO is watching Angelica Snowden September 19, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adrian Portelli’s rationale for moving to Dubai, at least in his telling, is pretty simple. Australia is “chasing away success”, according to the Melbourne-born billionaire, and entrepreneurs like him will keep leaving with one-way tickets because of exceedingly harsh tax settings. “I don’t trust the government,” Portelli told Karl Stefanovic in a new episode of the broadcaster’s controversial podcast. “They’ve really come down on me. Billionaire Adrian Portelli has moved to Dubai, and told Karl Stefanovic he doesn’t “trust” the Australian government. AAP “I’ve had regulatory issues to ATO [Australian Taxation Office] issues, and I just can’t handle it.” Portelli has more than 1 million followers on social media and in August, he told them he was relocating to the Middle East, in response to this year’s federal budget, and its sweeping changes to capital gains and property taxes that sparked warnings that innovation in Australia would be stifled.

Advertisement

Critics, including other young entrepreneurs, united to lobby against changes to capital gains taxes for business. Broadly, Portelli and Stefanovic’s discussion suggested wealthy Australians could vote with their feet and shift their lives and their businesses overseas, to countries where the regulatory burden is less prohibitive. Related Article Federal budget How a meme war with tech bros derailed Labor’s budget narrative Portelli is doing so and more are intending to follow his lead, according to Victoria Wells, a Melbourne lawyer who started her firm, Ape Law, in the United Arab Emirates in 2022. Last month, Wells and partner Stephan Roberto, along with Bali-based influencer couple Matt Cameron and Felicity Morgan, launched the business “Project Get Out”, to capitalise on Australians – particularly those working in tech – wanting to shift overseas. They received 1000 inquiries shortly after launching – just as Portelli went viral for his move.

Advertisement

But experts warn that it is not always straightforward for relocating Australians to cash in on lower tax rates. Deakin Business School lecturer Dr Kerui Zhai said Australia’s higher personal income taxes and the changes to capital gains tax were among the incentives for entrepreneurs to relocate to the UAE, where they could obtain “significant tax savings”. But he pointed out that companies with income largely derived from Australia would “probably still be subject to Australian corporate tax”. Dubai has been competing with Singapore and Bali to entice expats overseas, expats say. Bloomberg About 25,000 Australians live and work in Dubai. Expats from across the world comprise about 88 per cent of the broader UAE population, which hovered at 11 million in 2025, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. While some have left due to the war in Iran, Professor Sunita Jogarajan, from the University of Melbourne Law School, said there was a long-term increase in Australians making the move since the pandemic, with destinations such as Bali and Singapore also spruiking tax benefits to attract expats.

Advertisement

“I can see it from the cases going through the Administrative Review Tribunal. I have been in tax more than 20 years. There just was not as many [cases related to Australians’ tax status] as before,” Jogarajan said. Tribunal records show the ATO has indeed been pursuing Australians living overseas deemed to be tax residents to pay their share, regardless of where they are. ‘I’ve had regulatory issues to ATO issues, and I just can’t handle it.’ Adrian Portelli Engineer Trong Quy sought a refund of $524,943.29 from the tax office for the period between 2016 and 2020 because he claimed Dubai was his primary place of residence. But in March last year, he lost his final bid for a refund, as the tribunal ruled he was a resident of Australia. The tribunal judgment said: “Despite not treating Australia as his home in the relevant years, the applicant maintained connections with Australia that are objectively inconsistent with his ‘abandoning’ residence in Australia and making Dubai a ‘permanent’ (in the sense of not temporary) home.”

Advertisement

These connections included that Quy’s family home was in Perth, where his wife and daughters lived. Quy also acknowledged that he left other personal belongings in Australia “including winter clothing (not required in Dubai’s climate) and two guitars that he had been restoring”. Related Article Gambling Adrian Portelli’s giveaway business to be outlawed Earlier this year, oil and gas executive Ragnar Bulie won against the ATO, after it sought to make him pay tax on income earned in Singapore between 2018 and 2022. Bulie, who is from Norway and owns property in Australia, lived in Singapore during that time while his wife and children resided in Australia. He was earning about $700,000 per year, according to the tribunal’s judgment. “Mr Bulie’s economic and personal relations to Singapore were, in composite, stronger than his economic and personal relations to Australia during the relevant period,” the tribunal ruled.

Advertisement

Portelli earned his estimated $1.44 billion fortune – according to The Australian Financial Review’s Rich List – from his subscription-based lottery business that recently expanded into petrol stations. Before his move overseas, the federal government unveiled legislation to outlaw his business model. Discussing his plans for a new business, a “streamlined way for Australians to import goods”, Portelli told Stefanovic “they froze my accounts”. “I couldn’t pay my wages, I couldn’t pay staff. I couldn’t pay my bills. They just froze it all,” he said, without explaining exactly who took the action against him. “My accountant said he has never seen anything like this. He genuinely said they have abused their power.

Advertisement

“They are chasing young entrepreneurs, very talented [Australians]. People of wealth and success are moving. They are fleeing.” Related Article Petrol prices Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works In the UAE, corporate income is taxed at 9 per cent and there is no personal income tax. In Australia, companies pay a tax rate of at least 25 per cent, and personal income rates top out at 45 per cent for the most well-paid Australians. Jogarajan, who acknowledged she did not know how Portelli’s business was structured, suggested the billionaire could still be treated as an Australian resident for tax purposes. “Foreign residents are taxed in Australia on any money they make in Australia,” she said. “That’s the kind of thing people pay lawyers to get advice on.”

Advertisement

Portelli did not respond to a request for comment. Speaking generally, Jogarajan said: “You really need to move and have a home overseas and not have those connections to Australia. “One of the big issues is if the family doesn’t move. The individual might be in Australia for a short number of days, say 30 or 60 days, and not typically be considered a resident here, if their family and children are still here.” Crypto lawyer Victoria Wells began a business, “Project Get Out”, to advise Australians moving to Dubai. Wells’ “Project Get Out” seeks to advise on relocation and tax residency issues for Australian founders, investors and high-net-worth families. She said the venture wasn’t “about engineering arrangements to avoid Australian tax”.

Advertisement

“Tax is legitimately one consideration in that decision, alongside lifestyle, family, business opportunity, regulation and access to markets – but it shouldn’t be the decision itself. I often say that tax should be one coordinate on the map, not the compass,” Wells said. Wells contemplated her exit from Australia years before the latest military action in the Middle East. After the price of crypto crashed in 2022, which coincided with news that the asset would no longer be treated as a foreign currency, and hit with capital gains tax in Australia, Wells said many founders and crypto firms left Australia. Wells and partner Stephan Roberto. “That was really the writing on the wall for me. My friends and my peers were leaving. I was like, OK, I have to figure this out. Are there going to jobs in crypto in Australia? No. Are there going to be clients in crypto in Australia? No, they are also leaving,” she said. During the past 3½ years operating her Dubai-based law firm, Wells specialises in financial services, international arbitration and crypto. She said the business had reported exponential growth from clients seeking to domicile their companies in the UAE.

Advertisement

Since launching “Project Get Out”, Wells said she continued to clock 200 inquiries a day. “Adrian Portelli announced his departure from Australia, it was picked up and got a lot of press. [Meanwhile], the work that I do, naturally puts me front and centre for a lot of Australians looking at making an exit to the UAE specifically,” she said. Morgan, one of her Australian co-founders, is an influencer who moved to Bali two years ago. Her business, Felicity Morgan Coaching, was liquidated last September. According to the liquidator’s report in December, Morgan owed the ATO $774,118.65 in unpaid liabilities. The report also said Morgan received a director’s loan from the company for $1.08 million, which the liquidator requested be repaid. Morgan said: “The current status is incorrect, however, things take time to show on the system.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. The final hurdle has been cleared for Peter V’landys to become the NRL’s first executive chairman after club chairs offered their unanimous support for the move. The chairs of the clubs and state leagues took part in a phone hook-up on Saturday morning to discuss the ascension of V’landys to the new role. While Melbourne chair Matt Tripp and Wests Tigers counterpart Barry O’Farrell sent their apologies, all other officials backed the move during a half-hour conversation that began at 10:30am. Peter V’landys will become the NRL’s first executive chairman. Oscar Colman The appointment is expected to be rubber-stamped at a board meeting of the Australian Rugby League Commission scheduled for Wednesday. The role will give V’landys unprecedented control over the game, but the club and state heads feel there are sufficient guardrails in place to ensure protections. His tenure will be for an initial three-year term, a move V’landys himself proposed to ensure good governance.

Advertisement

If there is a dispute between V’landys and the clubs and states, they will be able to negotiate with a lead independent director who will be tasked to help resolve the impasse. While that role won’t be filled until V’landys ascends to his position, sources not authorised to speak publicly said ARL commissioners Peter Beattie and Gary Weiss are the leading contenders. Peter V’landys presents the minor premiership to Penrith earlierr this month. Getty Images Once V’landys takes the job, he will set a date to finish at Racing NSW, where he has been the chief executive for 22 years. V’landys is becoming executive chairman without calling a vote of clubs and states to amend the game’s constitution, which states that commissioners cannot be the CEO or an employee. Instead, he is relying on clause 53 of the document, which allows for the creation of other positions “from time to time” which can be occupied by members of the commission.

Advertisement

The sidestepping of constitutional change could be tested in court, but the unanimous support he received on Saturday suggests the key stakeholders have confidence in the direction V’landys is leading the game. The meeting was convened by South Sydney Rabbitohs chair Nick Pappas, who has been liaising with V’landys and the Commission about the move. “There was broad consensus among the clubs and the states,” Pappas said. “We have no objection to Peter taking that position – in fact we welcome it … There are some issues that require clarification in relation to guardrails around the position to ensure governance at the highest level, which is what Peter wants as well. “We are not at cross purposes on this … there is nothing that would act as an obstacle to him taking up that position.” V’landys has been acting as NRL chief for the past two months, having taken four months long-service leave from Racing NSW to fill the gap when Andrew Abdo departed for Tennis Australia.

It is a rare occurrence in Australian sport, where there is generally a separation of powers between the management and the board. The title provides V’landys even greater authority than the heads of US sports such as NBA commissioner Adam Silver and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, who are answerable to team owners. His elevation to executive chairman has raised governance concerns with some in the game, not about V’landys personally, but about a single figure wielding such control.

Washington: Denmark, the United States and Greenland are expected to sign an agreement that will allow the US to increase its military presence in the Danish territory and ban adversaries such as Russia and China from building bases or making sensitive investments there. The agreement was simultaneously announced by all three parties and will be signed at the United Nations next week when world leaders converge on New York for the UN General Assembly’s high-level meetings. Greenlanders protest in front of the US consulate in the capital, Nuuk, in January. Getty Images US President Donald Trump claimed the deal as a significant win, after making Arctic security a key plank of his foreign policy agenda. But he frightened European allies with his demands for US control of Greenland, and his threats to perhaps take the Danish territory by force. Based on details provided by a US State Department official, the deal stops well short of giving the US control over Greenland, but expands American access and puts explicit, permanent restrictions on the presence of NATO adversaries.

Advertisement

It guaranteed the US “complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent”, the State Department official said, including permanent access, basing and overflight rights. Related Article Mining Trump has big hopes for Greenland – Australia just gave him a reality check “This agreement ensures the necessary US military presence in Greenland permanently, allowing the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as required.” Under the deal, a non-NATO country would not be allowed to build a military base or maintain a troop presence in Greenland, and only the US and its allies could make sensitive investments in Greenland. The US had raised concerns about Chinese investments in the territory, although experts have said these claims are inflated, with most of China’s purported projects there failing or never materialising.

Advertisement

“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” the State Department official said. Related Article Analysis

Immigration Denmark’s new Iron Lady wants more missiles and fewer migrants. Will Europe follow her lead? Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen welcomed what she described as a “great agreement” between the three parties, which would strengthen their collective security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The deal also recognised the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, she noted, as well as the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination. Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen branded the deal a “joyous” agreement that benefited all involved. His statement with Frederiksen noted the deal would need to be ratified by the relevant national parliaments, such as Greenland’s Inatsisartut.

Advertisement

Trump, meanwhile, called it a “dream come true” and said the US would immediately begin developing a large military presence in an appropriate part of the territory. “For over 100 years, [US] Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said on social media. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.” Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen (left) and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen in 2025. AP Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who played a key role in the negotiations, called it a “huge win” for the US and the American people. “Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he said.

Advertisement

“This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.” America’s military presence in Greenland was already enabled by the 1951 Defence of Greenland Agreement, which gave the US the ability to operate and maintain bases in certain areas by agreement. title: Australia's push to join the UN Security Council

Anthony Albanese has arrived in California ahead of talks with tech giant Apple and an online safety push at the United Nations.

title: How much the age pension is rising — and a hit to your next holiday
text:
You may be aware that interest rates are likely to rise again in Australia, but did you know they may increase twice this year?

Planning a trip overseas soon? Be prepared to pay more to fly

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) warned this week that airfares will continue to climb as oil prices bounce higher and the war in the Middle East drags on.

In its Domestic Airline Competition in Australia report, it also revealed just how concentrated the market is locally.

Qantas Group, which also owns Jetstar, dominates with a 65.2 per cent share, Virgin Australia 33.3 per cent and Rex just 1.5 per cent.

"We'll be watching closely," ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gotlieb told me on the SBS On the Money podcast.

"We want to make sure they keep independently setting prices and independently make commercial decisions despite these challenging conditions."

Cass-Gotlieb said that while airlines may navigate higher jet fuel prices by cutting capacity, which means fewer seats in the sky, relief might come in time as Sydney's second airport comes online.

"What Western Sydney (International) will introduce is more available slots for take-off and landings and that can assist with new entrant airlines which we are hoping to see."

The Western Sydney International Airport is scheduled to commence commercial passenger services in October.

If global central banks sneeze, will the RBA catch the same cold?

Well, the reality is the Reserve Bank was already lifting official interest rates earlier this year before many other global central banks, because Australia was experiencing inflationary pressures before the war in the Middle East started.

But now, global central banks have started addressing price pressures relating to higher oil prices by lifting interest rates.

Last week, the Bank of Japan boosted rates to a 31-year high, while the US Federal Reserve also moved higher for the first time in more than three years.

So while Australian interest rates don't always move in tandem, economists say the world economy is now facing the same inflationary pressures.

Investment bank UBS became the latest to change its forecast and is now expecting two more RBA rate rises this year, taking the official cash rate to 4.8 per cent, with the first to come at the next meeting at the end of this month.

It blames three things: a change in tune from global central banks which are now lifting rates; higher oil prices stemming from the war in the Middle East; and large investments in artificial intelligence.

title: 'Temper tantrum': Why European countries are moving gold out of the US
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Donald Trump loves gold so much he has made it a symbol of his presidency.

Gold signage stands outside the Oval Office, gilded ornaments sit on its fireplace, and walls and ceilings now feature gold embellishments.

But while Trump may see gold as a visual shorthand for wealth and success, recent moves by France and the Netherlands to shift their gold reserves out of the United States may signal the exact opposite.

This month, the Netherlands announced it had transferred 86 tonnes of gold — equivalent to almost 7,000 bars — from vaults in the US and Canada to the Bank of England in London.

Although the transfer of around 59 tonnes of this was achieved by trading gold in New York for gold in London, more than 27 tonnes were physically moved.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The De Nederlandsche Bank said it was motivated by "increasing geopolitical unrest".

"Keeping a larger share of the gold reserves in London strengthens the function of gold as an anchor of trust," the bank said in a statement on 2 September.

US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office launching the "Trump Gold Card", a visa program that allows foreign nationals permanent residency and a pathway to US citizenship. Source: Getty / The Washington Post / Demetrius Freeman

The move follows France's announcement earlier this year that it had also shifted 129 tonnes of its gold from New York.

Some countries have been buying more gold in recent years, driving up the volume held by central banks. Between 2018 and 2025, reserves increased by 8.5 per cent.

During the same period, the price of gold has skyrocketed, increasing the market value of these reserves by 268 per cent, according to the International Monetary Fund.

Some experts say the moves could reflect concerns about the stability of institutions the world has relied on for decades.

Why do countries buy gold?

A country generally holds gold as part of its reserve assets, which act as a financial safety net. Reserves can help maintain the value of currency, protect against financial crises, and ensure countries can pay for imports and meet international debt repayments.

Australia's central bank, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), holds 80 tonnes of gold as part of its reserve assets, alongside government bonds from other countries.

Australia stores around 6,450 gold bars in London as part of its reserve. These ABC Bullion bars made in Sydney match the standard "Good Delivery" specifications set by the London Bullion Market Association and weigh around 12.4 kilograms each. Each bar is worth about $2.4 million each, according to spot prices on 15 September. The RBA stores hold four gold bars in Australia as part of its reserve. Source: SBS News

While Australia's gold reserves have largely remained unchanged since 1997, there's been a shift among other central banks such as China, India, Poland and Türkiye, which have started to favour buying gold over US government bonds.

Poland has significantly increased its gold reserves over the last 20 years, building it up from just 14 tonnes in 1996 to more than 630 tonnes by mid-2026.

Scott French, a senior lecturer at the University of NSW's school of economics, says gold is a commodity with intrinsic value that tends to increase over time.

No-one's ever going to default on gold.

This makes it a safe asset that generally doesn't lose its value even when interest rates are high, unlike government bonds.

The disadvantage of gold, however, is that it doesn't provide any income.

"Gold just sits there and doesn't produce anything; it doesn't pay interest."

Gold v bonds

One reason US government bonds are popular among investors, beyond their status as safe assets, is that they generate regular interest income.

Bonds are issued by governments to borrow money. If you buy a bond, the country pays you a fixed interest rate (known as a coupon) and will also repay the original amount you lent (the principal) when the bond matures.

The US Treasury market is the largest government bond market in the world, and US government bonds (known as Treasuries) are considered one of the safest financial assets.

This is because the US government has a long history of meeting its debt obligations, and it can also raise money by increasing taxes if it needs to generate additional income — something that is not available to companies.

READ MORE Australian families could be sitting on a goldmine, but many are torn about selling

But if inflation and interest rates rise — as they are currently in the US — the income received in interest from the bond will be less valuable, which also makes the bond more difficult to sell.

John Hawkins, a senior lecturer at the University of Canberra, says investors tend to buy gold when they are worried about rising interest rates and government debt, which can leave countries struggling to pay back bonds.

"[Gold] is one of the few alternatives to a government bond," the former RBA economist says.

Maintaining a stockpile of gold bullion within a country's own borders also makes these physical assets harder to seize and more secure than intangible financial assets.

Hawkins says global examples of assets being frozen may have highlighted the risks of storing physical assets overseas. He points to the seizure of Russia's foreign-held assets, including money held in bank accounts, following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Why are countries moving gold out of the US?

Securing greater control over assets may have been a factor in France's decision to sell the 129 tonnes of gold it had stored in New York last financial year. The country bought back the same amount of gold based in Europe and has stored this with the rest of its reserve in a vast underground vault known as the 'Souterraine' in Paris.

This gives it direct control over 2,437 tonnes of gold, the fourth-largest gold reserve in the world after the US, Germany and Italy (excluding the International Monetary Fund).

Gold reserves at the Banque de France. Source: Getty / Sygma / Pierre Perrin

Unlike France, the Netherlands opted to move some of its US-held gold to London rather than store it domestically. Around 37 per cent of the country's reserves also remain in the US and Canada.

London is an attractive place to store gold as it's a hub where buyers and sellers can trade large volumes of the metal. It also hosts major gold storage vaults, including those linked to the Bank of England.

The London bullion market is regarded as the world's largest gold trading centre and sets the LBMA Gold Price benchmark.

"If you have gold in London, you can mobilise it more quickly, more effectively, more easily," Nicholas Frappell, the global head of institutional markets at Australia's ABC Refinery, says.

The vast majority of Australia's 80-tonne gold reserve is stored at the Bank of England.

The Bank of England controls major gold storage vaults. Source: Getty / In Pictures / Mike Kemp

An RBA spokesperson says storing its gold there gives the RBA ready access to the gold market, as most market participants prefer to take delivery in London.

"The Bank of England provides a very secure and cost-effective storage location for central banks and other market participants," they said.

While these factors may have played a part in the decisions by France and the Netherlands to move gold out of the US, Hawkins says concerns around the erratic leadership of US President Trump may have also been a motivating factor.

[Trump's] threatened all sorts of measures against European countries if they don't do what he likes.

"So they're worried that some sort of temper tantrum … might lead to him somehow seizing the gold that's held in New York that's owned by those countries."

Questions over US stability

Hawkins says countries moving gold out of the US could be interpreted as "a decrease in confidence" in the US.

"I think the impact over the last few years is basically down to people not having confidence in the stability of the US and that's basically down to Trump."

Along with gold, central banks also hold foreign currencies in their reserve assets. Data shows foreign reserves of the US dollar appear to be declining.

In 2000, the US dollar made up 71 per cent of global foreign exchange reserves held by central banks, according to Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves data.

While the US remains the world's dominant reserve currency, it now only makes up around 57 per cent of reserves.

The US dollar was backed by gold until 1971. Source: Getty / CFOTO / Future Publishing

French says confidence in financial systems is very important, as most countries now have 'fiat currencies' — a term that describes government-issued currencies not backed by gold or any other physical commodity.

It relies on the belief in stability of the government that's backing that currency, and trust in the rest of society to continue to accept that currency.

The US dollar used to be backed by gold under the Bretton Woods system, with other countries linking their currencies to the dollar. This helped establish the global trading system and gave the US dollar prominence, which endures today despite it no longer being backed by gold.

One of the reasons why the Chinese renminbi is unlikely to become a dominant reserve currency, despite China's economic strength, is due to perceived uncertainty. It currently makes up just 2 per cent of foreign currency reserves held by central banks.

While there is confidence in the Chinese government's ability to pay its bonds, French says the country's institutions are seen as beholden to the Chinese Communist Party and President Xi Jinping.

"You're putting a lot of faith in one person to act responsibly and you never know what that one person is going to do, so that makes it a riskier long-term investment," French says.

Tight political control of Chinese institutions under the leadership of President Xi Jinping makes investment more risky. Source: Getty / Evan Vucci / Pool

What happens after Trump?

For now, the US dollar remains the proverbial 'gold standard', despite lingering concerns over Trump's volatility.

The president's comments aimed at exerting control over institutions, including repeatedly attacking the Federal Reserve for not cutting interest rates, have undermined faith in the independence of US decision-making, French says.

He has also put the US on a "very precarious fiscal path" by cutting taxes last year without significantly cutting US spending, at a time when the country has a $60 trillion budget deficit, which has raised questions about its ability to repay bonds.

But French says the US Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates this week despite criticism from Trump is a positive sign of its credibility.

Ironically, one of the best things for the Trump administration … is for the central bank to do what [the president] doesn't want them to do.

French doesn't think Trump has done enough damage yet for the US dollar to be dumped as the global reserve currency.

"We're almost halfway into the second Trump administration … I wouldn't expect to see anything catastrophic over the next couple of years," he says.

"So really the question is, what happens after Donald Trump?"

French says if the next administration behaves responsibly, there's no reason the US dollar won't remain the dominant global currency for the next couple of decades.

"If further administrations continue on the same path, then we could be in trouble for multiple reasons."

title: Nearly two million Quest Apartment Hotels customers affected by data breach
text:
In brief Quest Apartment Hotels says the information of nearly two millions customers was compromised in a data breach.

The data includes credit card, passport, and Medicare numbers.

Personal information of nearly two million Quest Apartment Hotels customers has been compromised in a data breach, including credit card, passport and Medicare numbers.

Last month, the accommodation provider identified a cyberattack on a database system via a vulnerability in a third-party technology provider.

David Mansfield, the managing director of The Ascott Limited, which owns Quest Apartment Hotels, provided an update this week, saying a forensic data analysis revealed information relating to approximately 1,991,613 customers was affected.

The majority of information related to names and contacts, but also included:

Vehicle registration numbers: 225,300

Passport and/or driver licence numbers (the number only; no scanned copies of ID documents were affected): 104,268

Credit card numbers (no CVV, including expired credit cards): 297,739

Credit card numbers (with CVV, including expired credit cards): 46,727

Date of birth: 3,328

NDIS number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 271

Medicare card number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 46

All the information relates to records from before June 2025.

Mansfield said the company was contacting those affected directly to inform them of which category they were in, the steps they could take, and available support.

"I recognise the concern this incident has caused. On behalf of Quest, I sincerely apologise to those who have been affected," he said.

Quest said it first identified an outage on its website on 17 August, with investigation revealing "a malicious attack" had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party service provider's software.

The company is advising customers to remain alert for suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls, particularly communications requesting personal, financial or account information.

READ MORE Australian patient details exposed in GP network cyberattack

Quest said it was cooperating with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian Cyber Security Centre and Victoria Police.

Last year's Annual Cyber Threat Report warned cyberattacks were a growing problem in Australia, with financial losses, ransomware attack frequency, and the number of reported data breaches all increasing.

After a major data breach involving millions of Optus customers in 2022, the federal government overhauled privacy laws, requiring companies to destroy or actively de-identify personal information as soon as it was no longer needed.

Incident raises data concerns

Paul Watters, chief executive of Cyberstronomy, which provides cyber risk expertise, said all businesses needed to have a clear understanding of the personal data they hold and why.

"Often, this is not the case," he told SBS News.

"Quest says all of the affected information came from records dating from before June 2025. That immediately raises a governance question: for each category of information, why was it still being retained?"

He said the incident could serve as a lesson for organisations.

"Audit your data holdings. Know what you have, where it is, why you are retaining it, how long you need it, and when it should be deleted or de-identified. Data you no longer hold cannot be stolen in a breach," he said.

Belinda Barnet, a Swinburne University data privacy expert, told SBS News the latest incident raised concerns about the type of data some companies were still retaining.

"Companies like Quest don't need to retain your passport after you've actually identified yourself," she said.

"We really need to have more public discussion about how [companies are] going to destroy information that's no longer needed."

title: The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality
text:
In brief Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said "upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising".

It reaffirmed expectations that the board would hike rates again at this month's meeting.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) fears about inflation have materialised, its governor Michele Bullock says, which could force it to raise interest rates again.

Her comments during a parliamentary hearing on Friday morning reaffirmed expectations that the central bank would hike rates for a fourth time this year at its upcoming board meeting in late September.

Inflation was too high, but the key question for the RBA at that meeting would be whether the bank's three rate rises to date were enough to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time, Bullock said.

At its last meeting in August, the RBA forecast that inflation would return to the middle of its target range of 2-3 per cent by the end of 2027.

Even that was not assured, with inflation more likely to overshoot the bank's forecasts than undershoot it.

If that proved to be the case, more rate hikes might be warranted, the RBA board said at the time.

"Developments since then suggest that, although growth in the Australian economy is slowing, some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising," Bullock said on Friday.

The Middle East conflict, the AI boom, and extreme weather events have added to pressure on energy, food, and tech prices, she said.

"There is little sign of resolution in the Middle East conflict. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add directly to inflation."

The benchmark Brent crude price remained above US$104 ($146) a barrel, despite a modest sell-off in oil overnight on news that Saudi Arabia plans to bring its East-West pipeline back online in a reduced capacity following attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces.

But as businesses increasingly saw no end in sight to the war and price increases, they were growing more inclined to pass on costs to consumers, which risked making inflation more persistent, Bullock said.

After inflation came in hotter than expected in July, money markets have raised the chance for a September rate rise above 80 per cent, with two hikes fully priced in by March.

Higher-for-longer interest rates and fuel prices would hit economic growth, but that has been swamped by the AI boom, which has pushed up demand in a way the RBA did not foresee.

"Just back from the US and in addition to ... the upside risk of inflation from the Middle East, what is also very striking is how strong the AI and tech boom is and has been," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said.

"That's not just true in the US; it's true in the Asia Pacific region as well, who are of course our closest trading partners, and our forecasts for global growth have been repeatedly surprised on the upside."

Given Australia's productivity malaise, a period of slower growth was needed to bring inflation down, Bullock said.

The nation's deepening housing downturn would help take some steam out of the economy, but while prices have fallen in most capital cities, they remain about 50 per cent higher than in early 2020.

title: 'I am learning': HYROX athlete apologises and withdraws after viral defecation incident
text:
In Brief Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has issued an apology after soiling herself during a HYROX race in Beijing.

The incident prompted HYROX to formally change its rulebook to withdraw racers if their faeces pose a "contamination risk".

The Australian athlete at the centre of the HYROX defecation controversy has apologised and retroactively withdrawn from the race after footage of the incident went viral internationally.

Social media footage showed Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk, who holds the women's HYROX solo pro world record, competing at exercise stations with faeces on her legs during a race in Beijing over the weekend.

She finished the race and won despite the incident.

In a statement posted to Instagram on Thursday night, Wietrzyk apologised for her decision to continue competing.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she wrote.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track.

"I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused."

Wietrzyk also announced that she would forfeit the points she earned as the competition winner.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," she said.

"On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned."

Ending her statement, Wietrzyk said: "Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support.

"It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."

Days of silence following controversy

The Instagram statement came almost a week after the incident.

HYROX is a fitness and endurance race that combines 8km of running with exercises such as rowing, sled pushes and wall balls, carried out in indoor exhibition halls.

Wietrzyk initially shared a selfie on her Instagram story after the race, which showed her lying down with an intravenous line in her arm. It was captioned: "Go hard or go home they say ... a win is a win".

Multiple media outlets also reported that Wietrzyk's major sponsor, Puma, was distancing itself from the athlete after their collaborative line appeared to be quietly removed from the sportswear giant's website a day ago.

The page has since been restored online, with a Puma spokesperson telling CBC News that some landing pages were "unintentionally taken offline".

Incident prompts HYROX rule change

The incident has prompted backlash and criticism of HYROX's health and safety standards, with many wondering why Wietrzyk was permitted to continue competing with fecal matter visibly running down her legs.

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste issued a statement earlier this week apologising to those "directly or indirectly" affected by the incident, "as well as to everyone who felt we did not handle the situation like we should have".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately to the incident," Fürste said. "In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

Fürste said event processes have since been improved, including "rulebook changes" and "new rules and procedures" that he said will "prevent situations like this from happening again".

"We learn and try to get better everyday," he said.

In the updated HYROX rulebook, a racer can be withdrawn on medical grounds if their "blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers … in line with HYROX’s medical and hygiene SOPs".

Gut issues and endurance sports

According to research by Monash University, strenuous exercise lasting two hours or more — particularly running — appears to exacerbate gut disturbances.

Researchers estimate 30 to 70 per cent of athletes experience gastrointestinal symptoms, with endurance athletes particularly susceptible.

Bec Hoschke, a former professional triathlete and Ironman champion who now coaches endurance athletes in Sydney, told SBS News earlier this week that gut health can be a "highly sensitive thing for many endurance athletes".

She said the HYROX incident was a "very difficult situation" for the parties involved: the competition, the athlete and her competitors.

"Athletes make enormous sacrifices for international competition," she said. "For some athletes, it's their living."

She said the issue was not only one of public health and hygiene but also of the health and well-being of the athlete involved.

"I can't imagine the mental impact all of this is having on someone. I think she's only in her early 20s as well. It's enormously confronting for someone to have to deal with at that age."

title: The EU wants a new kind of member — and Australia could be in the mix
text:
In brief Canada's leader has welcomed the proposal to become an "associate member" of the European Union.

The president of the European Parliament hinted that Australia and New Zealand could be next.

Australia and New Zealand could follow in Canada's footsteps to become "associate members" of the European Union, a top EU official has suggested.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, in an interview with Europe Today, specifically brought up Australia and New Zealand as examples of countries that could deepen their relationships with the alliance.

Metsola said the EU had different models for its relationships with other countries, from full membership to participation in the European Economic Area, and was also looking to deepen ties with partners such as Canada — a model she expected other countries to pursue.

"I don't doubt that that will also include other countries that will come," she said.

"We've already seen it, both in terms of legislation that we pass, where we see partners from across the world — Australia, New Zealand being some examples — of saying, look, we want to deepen our relationship."

"We're doing it in terms of trade. We're doing it in terms of conversation on what we do with social media, with children, with critical raw materials, alliances that can be forged."

"If we can do more things with our friends, then let's do them."

Europe and Canada 'stronger together'

Canadian Prime ‌Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the proposal of becoming an "associate member" of the EU, saying Europe and Canada are stronger together ‌and should deepen ties to protect their citizens' prosperity.

"Europe and Canada are each strong. Europe and Canada are even stronger together," Carney told the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday.

"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners."

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing ‌resilience so that ‌no one can ⁠control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

READ MORE EU proposes landmark associate membership for Canada

Hours earlier, US President Donald Trump threatened to take action against the EU if it moved forward with European Commission President Ursula von der ‌Leyen's proposal of associate membership for Canada.

Both the EU and Canada have been facing stiff rivalry and pressure from the Trump administration on trade, among other matters, and from an increasingly assertive China.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, ⁠I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many ‌things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina.

"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll ‌put very heavy tariffs on Europe," he added.

The European Commission said the proposal — which is yet to be fleshed out and will need to be approved by EU member states to go forward — was not a hostile act.

"As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength," said Olof Gill, a European Commission spokesperson.

Speaking in the European Parliament on Thursday, ‌Carney made clear he, like the EU, sought deeper ties and "welcomed" the ambition to become an associate member.

"We are not fair-weather allies," he said.

"We believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."

Among areas in which he said Canada would want closer ties with the EU he mentioned seeking strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space, and payments.

He also mentioned digital trade and building more secure broadband connections between Europe ⁠and Asia via their common geography.

title: Burke's pitch to worried farmers as he warns of migration overhaul risk
text:
IN BRIEF The home affairs minister says there will be impacts on industry from the migration changes.

He also suggested farmers should consider hiring Pacific workers amid concerns over backpacker labour shortages.

The Home Affairs Department has engineered a slowdown in backpacker visas to reduce arrivals and is now urging farmers to consider hiring Pacific workers to pick their crops.

The National Farmers' Federation has led a campaign to axe visa bottlenecks amid growing industry anxiety that fruits and other crops will wither on trees without the labour force needed to harvest them.

The agricultural sector is warning the shortages will increase supermarket prices.

As the federal government moves to reduce arrivals to Australia, its visa overhaul includes introducing a ballot system for backpackers hoping to spend more than one year in Australia on a working holiday visa.

It will also cut the available long-term visas. Backpackers from the United Kingdom will be exempt from the requirements because of the UK's free trade deal with Australia.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In an interview with SBS News, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has encouraged any horticulture businesses struggling to secure harvest workers to consider the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and Pacific workers.

"Our preferred agriculture visa has always been the PALM scheme, the Pacific workers visa. When I was employment minister, we did a lot to improve the rules to avoid worker exploitation on the Pacific, on the PALM visa," he said.

"At the time that we were improving those rules, we had some of the farm organisations say to us, 'If you do this, our members will just go and use backpackers.'"

He maintains there is a Pacific workforce ready to step in.

"Now, if the reason that people are more reliant on backpackers and refusing to use Pacific workers is because they're upset that we've ended exploitation in those areas, I think that is a very different question for a number of operators.

"That doesn't depict the whole of the farm sector, not for a minute, and a whole lot of them still use the Pacific Labour Scheme, but the Pacific Labour Scheme right now has extra capacity. Those extra workers are available."

'I can't quarantine any sector of Australia'

Burke said he can't quarantine any sector of the economy from the impacts of the migration shake-up.

The government wants to reduce the number of working holidaymakers, crack down on visa overstayers and tighten allowances for international students as part of its push to reduce migration numbers.

Farmers and the Nationals have been among the critics of changes set to affect backpackers, who the former rely on to pick fruit in the regions.

Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year under the system, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively.

Burke told SBS News there will be challenges for industry to adjust to the changes.

"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he said.

"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure —as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."

One in five international students to be impacted

The government's plan to stop some international students from bringing their families to Australia could affect about one in five people, amid warnings of an economic hit if some choose to study elsewhere.

International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia under the reforms.

PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students are exempt from the proposal.

Burke told SBS News around 19 per cent of the cohort bring in family members to Australia. It's unclear whether that includes PhD students, who are more likely to bring family than undergraduates.

"International students tend to be younger, and so family obligations are a very different issue," Burke said.

Asked whether the proposal, which could affect 19 per cent of the cohort, would amount to a major revenue hit for universities and the economy, Burke insisted demand for student spots will bridge any gap.

"It's actually not, for the very simple reason that at the moment, we have more students wanting to study in Australia than we have places," he said.

"Whereas for skilled workers, everyone who an employer can find, they take, because that's completely demand-driven. There's no planning level on temporary skilled visas at all.

"You don't have the same impact for students, nor do you have the same size of demand simply because people tend to be younger."

There are around 680,582 international students in Australia. About 295,000 new international students are due to commence next year, in student cap figures unchanged from this year.

Universities Australia welcomed the carve-out for PhD students, saying Australia was competing globally for researchers and highly-skilled people.

The Group of Eight representing Australia's research-intensive universities said it educated about half of PhD students — about 12,000, with half of those requiring secondary visas for dependants.

"Most of our undergraduate international students are quite young. They're ... 18, 19, 20, and many of them aren't coming here with their parents, frankly," CEO Vicki Thompson told ABC News.

Other measures that will affect students include preventing so-called 'visa hopping', with a new qualification scale to allow only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's, for example) to extend their visas.

title: 'A struggle every day': There's a hidden side to Australia's student visa debate
text:
IN BRIEF The government says the changes will help cut net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year.

Students and migration experts have raised concerns about how some of the new restrictions could affect migrants.

For almost nine years, Bashshar Khalid has been building a life in Australia.

He arrived as an international student in 2017, completed a three-year bachelor's degree in business and then a two-year master's degree before entering the workforce.

But graduating was only the beginning.

Khalid first moved onto a temporary graduate visa, known as a subclass 485, and recently secured a subclass 482 work visa after finding employment in sales.

He told SBS News that making the transition from international student to skilled worker was far from straightforward.

One of the biggest difficulties was convincing an employer to invest in someone whose ability to remain in Australia had an expiry date attached to it.

"We basically have to work twice as hard, or we just have to prove our skill set to our employers," he said.

At one point, Khalid's temporary graduate visa was approaching expiry while his employer-sponsored visa application was still being processed.

He moved onto a bridging visa while he waited for an outcome.

"Every day when you wake up, or every day you're going into the office to work, you're not sure whether the application will be approved or not ... It's basically a struggle every day."

Bashshar Khalid came to Australia as an international student in 2017 and recently secured a 482 work visa. Credit: Image: Supplied

Government's migration crackdown

Now, the federal government has announced another suite of changes aimed at tightening Australia's migration system and further reducing net overseas migration (NOM).

The changes include measures targeting so-called "visa hopping", restrictions on secondary applicants on most student visas and stronger measures to ensure people without valid visas leave Australia.

The government will also introduce a 'no further stay' condition on all visitor visas and crack down on migration agents it says knowingly support applications without merit.

Announcing the reforms on Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government was targeting people who would "never" meet the requirements for permanent residency but continued moving through the migration system to extend their stay.

"They effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.

Critics say the crackdown could limit legitimate study and work opportunities.

Khalid said he believes there should be a clearer distinction between people switching courses simply to stay in the country, and migrants legitimately progressing through study and skilled employment.

"We have contributed to the economy. We have paid our taxes. We have done everything right by the book," he said.

"There couldn't be one single hard and fast rule about everything.

"If they could genuinely prove that the change of career is more of a personal choice and not just for a visa hopping case, then I think they should be given a fair chance."

Former immigration department deputy secretary Abul Rizvi also supports reducing visa hopping but cautioned against applying restrictions too broadly.

"As a general rule, I think reducing visa hopping is a good idea," he said.

READ MORE Tony Burke set to unveil Labor's new migration plan amid working holiday visa concerns

"The question will be how broadly those measures are applied, because if they're applied too broadly, there will be unintended consequences."

Rizvi pointed to businesses that bring workers into Australia on business visas when they urgently need their skills while waiting for a skilled temporary visa to be processed.

If those transitions are restricted while skilled visa processing times remain lengthy, he said, businesses could face difficulties.

'It would have definitely affected my decision'

For Khalid, the uncertainty of Australia's migration system has already made planning a career difficult.

Khalid said policy changes could mean migrants made significant decisions based on one set of rules, only to find the pathway had shifted.

"If my pathway was not as clear ... it would have been a major decision for me whether I should stay on in the country or leave the country," he said.

Had the pathway been more restrictive when he was studying, Khalid said it "would have definitely affected" his decision.

His recently granted 482 visa now provides a potential pathway towards permanent residency.

"After spending a good amount of time in this country, you sort of feel like it's your second home," he said.

What will the changes mean for students with families?

The government's reforms also restrict secondary applicants on most student visas, potentially affecting students seeking to have family members join them in Australia.

Muath Alqarni, a Saudi master's degree student at the University of Melbourne, told SBS Arabic that he understood the government wanted greater control over migration involving international students' families but was concerned about broad restrictions.

"I recognise there is an issue with international students' families' immigration, and I understand that the federal government is trying to control it," he said.

"However, as an international student who used to live with his family, my situation is different."

Alqarni urged the government to examine the data and circumstances of different groups rather than applying broad measures.

"It's a lifetime chance for me to bring my family to Australia and spend a good time with them in Australia," he said.

Rizvi also raised concerns about students undertaking lengthy courses who may be affected by restrictions on bringing partners to Australia.

"If you're doing a four-year nursing degree or a five-year engineering degree or a six-year medicine degree and you're married, to be without your partner for four or six years is really, really difficult," he said.

He argued Australia risked losing some prospective students to competing destinations if they could not bring their partners.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Will the changes bring migration down?

The government says the reforms are designed to help bring NOM down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.

Rizvi believes those forecasts will probably be achieved if the changes are combined with the high student visa refusal rates he says have been in place since November 2025.

International students have played a significant role in recent movements in NOM, he said.

"The biggest increase in the big surge in net migration in 2023 was students, and the biggest reduction since then has been students," Rizvi said.

Burke said migration also needed to slow sufficiently for housing supply to "catch up", but rejected the suggestion migration itself was responsible for Australia's housing shortage.

"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.

"But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."

title: 'Absurd': Yoga teachers become an unlikely flashpoint in Australia's migration debate
text:
IN BRIEF The coalition has claimed that Australia was bringing in more yoga teachers than tradies.

Tony Burke addressed the claim at a National Press Club speech, saying it was a "silly" argument.

Amid an ongoing political battle over which party's at fault for a lack of housing and migration numbers, an unlikely target has emerged: yoga teachers.

Labor has been accused by the Opposition of prioritising bringing in instructors of the flexible exercise to Australia, over construction workers sorely needed to address a critical housing shortage.

The Coalition since 2024 has levelled claims against Labor of putting instructors for martial arts and yoga ahead of tradies like bricklayers, painters, roof tilers and stonemasons in the visa queue.

The origins of the political line of attack appeared to come from a Nine Newspaper report which said in 2024 that a federal agency, Jobs and Skills Australia, listed yoga teachers as a skill in demand. Former coalition MP Michael Sukkar highlighted the report on social media, saying: "Under Labor they'll be more Yoga teachers and less tradies!".

On Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke sought to put the claims to bed, once and for all.

"It is absurd," he told the National Press Club, saying it was among the "silliest of all" arguments.

Burke outlined that rather than deprioritising construction workers, the government had tripled the number it was bringing in, from 4,500 to 15,000.

"In the life of this government, the number of yoga teachers we have brought in is zero," he said.

"Zero. And yet this claim is constantly made about yoga teachers."

According to a fact check from Australian Associated Press (AAP) newswire, the opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg and colleagues made the claim a number of times in the past year, saying the government was bringing in more yoga teachers than construction workers.

"While this figure may include yoga teachers, it could also cover coaches of other sports such as basketball or cricket," it said in an August finding.

Yoga teachers came under the temporary skilled visa program in 2022 after the Morrison government signed a trade agreement with India. The places are reserved for Indian nationals under that deal.

"It's a tiny argument, but it is so constantly out there and so demonstrably wrong, it gives an indication as to how a debate like this can just run out of control," Burke said.

title: Cuts, punishment powers and a notable exception: Key changes in Labor's migration shake-up
text:
In brief The federal government has announced a suite of changes to Australia's immigration policy settings.

Working holidaymakers, visa overstayers and students are among those most affected.

The federal government has announced a shake-up of Australia's migration system, with visa-hoppers, overstayers, students, and backpackers targeted in the crackdown.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled the changes during a National Press Club address on Thursday, following weeks of delay, heated debate and speculation.

Burke began his speech by highlighting the contribution of migration to Australia, but acknowledging there were problems with the current policy settings.

Here's what you need to know:

What's changing?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Burke said the reforms are split into three parts: who arrives, who stays and who leaves.

Among the most consequential changes are those affecting students, backpackers, visa overstayers and visa hoppers.

International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia, with some exceptions for PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students.

The changes are not retrospective and apply only to future students.

"We're not going to be breaking up families on shore," he said.

As part of a so-called "visa-hopping" crackdown, Burke said the government will introduce a qualification scale, meaning only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's for example) will be able to extend their visas.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the changes at the National Press Club on Thursday. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

A ballot system and cap will be introduced for backpackers wishing to extend their visit to a second or third year.

Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively. This will not affect United Kingdom citizens under the rules of a free trade agreement.

The government has already slowed down the processing of working holiday visas, with applications now taking months to be approved. Burke said processing of second-and third-year visas will be restored to the previous, faster pace — with the exception of UK citizens, who are exempt from regional work requirements to secure a visa extension.

The number of UK backpackers has risen sharply since the free trade agreement came into effect in 2023, from about 17,000 in 2021 to just under 80,000 now.

People who overstay their visas, of whom there are about 77,000, will face tougher sanctions, including detention. The government is now looking for more facilities, compliance officers and beds.

Burke said this was a return to a pre-2015 model, when visa overstayers would be taken into detention, and within a few weeks, organise their own flight and leave.

"That didn't just affect them. It had a behavioural impact," he said.

However, he said it would not involve "the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries", an apparent reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, which have involved mass deportation operations, arrests, and third-country removals.

Powers to punish dodgy migration agents who help with applications they know have no merit will be expanded, including deregistration.

The points test, which determines which skilled migrants are admitted to Australia, will be revamped to treat construction-related qualifications as equivalent to university degrees.

Tweaks to ministerial directions will also prioritise visa applicants with in-demand skills, including in healthcare, construction, education and law enforcement.

Why the changes?

The government is trying to bring Australia's Net Overseas Migration, which represents population growth due to migration, down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027 and 225,000 each year thereafter, and to curb visa-hopping, "rorting" and "gaming" the system.

That figure has stubbornly exceeded Labor's forecasts since the party came to power in 2022, but Burke said migration was now tracking in line with its targets.

The Coalition wants the target to be about 170,000, in line with housing construction, and One Nation wants a 130,000-person-a-year cap.

Burke said immigrants were not to blame for Australia's housing crisis, but said immigration needed to slow down so that housing had a chance to catch up.

How are the changes being implemented?

Some of the changes will come under improved ministerial powers, but others may not become law because negotiations between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition leader Angus Taylor broke down in the week before Burke's address, dooming hope of getting reforms through the Senate.

Without parliament's approval, the government cannot proceed with restrictions on phoney asylum-seekers' claims.

But Burke insisted negotiations with the Coalition were ongoing and productive, and said: "We have put nothing forward that is a wedge to them."

What has the reaction been?

Kon Karapanagiotidis, CEO and founder of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, said the announced changes marked "a dark day for multicultural Australia".

"Today our government chose to turn on migrants, international students and people seeking asylum who have built lives here, contributed to this country and asked for nothing more than the chance to belong," he said in a statement.

The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) said changes to backpacker visas risked Australia's food security, farm safety and regional economies which rely heavily on working holidaymakers.

"This is not how serious policy is made. You do not switch off, slow down or redesign an important workforce pathway on the eve of harvest and expect farmers, contractors, processors and regional communities to absorb the damage," NFF president Hamish McIntyre said.

His comments were echoed by the NFF Horticulture Council executive officer Richard Shannon, who warned of a spike in food prices if the agricultural sector faced a worker shortfall.

"Backpackers doing harvest work in regional Australia are not the cause of housing shortages in our capital cities. They are the reason fruit gets picked, packed and onto supermarket shelves," he said.

Earlier this week, Universities Australia chief Luke Sheehy said political parties competing to cut international student numbers needed to be honest about what Australia would lose.

"A vote for dramatically fewer international students is a vote for a poorer, less skilled Australia," he said.

"You can't take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences."

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press
