title: Ed Sheeran rarely talks politics. The Macklemore controversy has put him at the centre of it
text:
IN BRIEF Sheeran says his concerts aren't a "political forum", but the Macklemore fallout has put that position under scrutiny.

What began with Macklemore saying "Free Palestine" on stage has grown into a wider dispute involving several artists.

Ed Sheeran has built one of the world's biggest music careers while largely avoiding one of the more divisive parts of modern celebrity: politics.

The English singer has spoken publicly about some causes over the years, including performing at a major benefit concert for Ukraine following Russia's 2022 invasion. But he has generally resisted using his concerts as a political platform, something he says is deliberate.

Now, Macklemore's removal from his United States tour has drawn Sheeran into a political debate he has largely sought to avoid.

In less than two weeks, Macklemore has made a high-profile pro-Palestinian speech while opening for Sheeran, been removed from his remaining US tour dates, and been followed out the door by four other acts.

Sheeran has insisted the decision to remove the American rapper wasn't his and says he spent days trying to prevent it.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But the fallout has nevertheless dragged the 35-year-old singer into a highly charged debate over the Israel-Gaza conflict, antisemitism and the role, or responsibility, of artists to use their platforms to take a political stand.

And it has forced Sheeran to publicly explain why, unlike Macklemore, he generally chooses not to.

"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," Sheeran wrote in a lengthy statement posted to Instagram this week.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

Embroiled in the controversy

The dispute began on 4 September, when Macklemore was performing as a support act on Sheeran's Loop Tour at a New Jersey stadium.

Introducing his 2024 protest song Hind's Hall, the rapper told the crowd that part of the reason he wanted to join the tour was to use its enormous stadium audiences to amplify his support for Palestinians.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine'," Macklemore said.

The following day, he again addressed the conflict, telling Jewish members of the audience that his criticism of Israel was not criticism of them.

The remarks sparked a backlash, with the Israeli-American Council launching a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from the tour, arguing Sheeran's stage should not be used for "one-sided political propaganda".

Macklemore has rejected accusations that his comments were antisemitic.

By Monday, he was off the tour. Promoter Messina Touring Group said venue owners hosting upcoming dates had indicated they would not allow shows featuring Macklemore to proceed.

Sheeran's attempt to stay out of politics

The episode has highlighted the starkly different approaches the two artists take to their public platforms.

Macklemore has become increasingly outspoken about Gaza and has framed speaking about Palestinians from the stage as a moral obligation.

Sheeran, meanwhile, said this week that people attending his concerts "do not expect a political forum".

"I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," he said.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace."

READ MORE Israeli minister calls for Oscar-winning film directors to be stripped of citizenship

Sheeran said he instead wants his shows to provide "safety and sanctuary" and bring together people from different backgrounds.

That doesn't mean Sheeran has always avoided political issues or humanitarian causes. In 2022, he performed at the televised Concert for Ukraine, which raised millions for people affected by Russia's invasion. He has also previously spoken publicly on issues including Brexit and LGBTQ+ equality.

But the singer has long resisted being characterised primarily as a political artist.

'I am not complicit'

Sheeran has also rejected suggestions he personally silenced Macklemore.

He said Macklemore had been allowed to choose his own setlist and that his contract for the tour was with the promoter.

Sheeran said he spent the week speaking with venues and was involved in discussions with promoters and activists on both sides in an effort to find a solution that would allow the tour to continue.

Ultimately, he said, the venues and promoter made the final decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran said.

"I am not complicit."

Artists walk away from Sheeran's tour

The dispute has now spread beyond Macklemore, with several artists withdrawing from Sheeran's tour in solidarity.

According to Reuters, singer-songwriter Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe have pulled out, while Irish band Beoga — which had been serving as Sheeran's touring band — is also leaving.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said.

Rowe and Beoga both invoked Ireland's history in explaining their decisions.

Sheeran said he had spent the week trying to find a way forward that would allow Macklemore (pictured) to remain on the tour, including speaking directly with venues, promoters and activists on both sides of the issue. Credit: Invision

Beoga said its members were "Irish people who understand colonialism" and pointed to their involvement with the Irish Artists for Palestine movement.

Rowe, who described Sheeran as a friend who had changed his life, said he could not stand by while powerful people silenced those who spoke out.

Lukas Graham described its withdrawal as a "difficult decision", while arguing that wealth should not determine who was able to participate in public debate.

Why was Macklemore removed?

Macklemore has long publicly supported Palestinians and criticised Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

In 2024, he released the protest song Hind's Hall in solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators and in memory of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who was killed in Gaza.

Macklemore has claimed New England Patriots NFL team owner Robert Kraft, whose Massachusetts stadium is hosting two upcoming Sheeran concerts, rallied stadium owners against his involvement in the tour.

READ MORE Australia sanctions Israeli extremists in response to violence in Palestine

Kraft has said he has dedicated significant time to fighting hate and antisemitism and felt a responsibility to intervene when he believed "that line has been crossed". Reuters reported Kraft had not publicly addressed Macklemore's specific claim that he rallied other stadium owners.

Pro-Israeli groups and US singer Pink, who is Jewish, have also criticised Macklemore, arguing comments made at concerts could compromise the safety of Jewish and pro-Israeli attendees.

Critics have also pointed to a 2014 appearance in which Macklemore wore a costume featuring a black wig, beard and fake hooked nose, which was criticised for invoking antisemitic stereotypes. Macklemore later apologised.

Macklemore has denied his recent comments were antisemitic, arguing that criticism of Israel's actions should not be conflated with antisemitism.

Sheeran's US tour is scheduled to resume in Philadelphia on 19 September.

NationalVictoriaLocal council An activist depicted a female councillor as Miss Piggy. A judge says it’s political speech Lachlan Abbott September 19, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A self-styled council watchdog has won an appeal against an intervention order granted to an inner-eastern Melbourne mayor after a judge ruled his social media posts, including one depicting her as Miss Piggy, were protected political speech. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston hailed the County Court judgment released late on Friday as a win for democratic scrutiny of elected officials, as it overturned the court order Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr was granted last year. Council Watch president Dean Hurlston (left) and Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr. Simon Schluter, Luis Enrique Ascui Magistrate Michelle Hodgson previously found “the gendered and personal undertones” of Hurlston’s posts and text messages to Sehr in recent years “crossed the line from fair commentary into targeted ridicule” that was intended to cause mental harm. But County Court judge Julie Clayton disagreed and on Friday threw out the personal safety intervention order against Hurlston.

Advertisement

Clayton found the magistrate’s interpretation of political commentary protected under Victorian law was too narrow and Hurlston’s posts were primarily motivated by concern about the City of Stonnington’s governance. Related Article CBD Council activist apologises – twice – after accusing councillor of sexual harassment “The personal integrity of politicians, quite apart from their policy positions, is a legitimate subject for news and current affairs,” Clayton wrote. On Saturday, Hurlston criticised Stonnington chief executive Dale Dickson for claiming the magistrate’s initial ruling was a “landmark court decision” before it was overturned. “The council’s triumphal public statement now stands as a monument to poor judgment,” Hurlston said.

Advertisement

“This case should concern every journalist, activist, ratepayer and community watchdog. If robust criticism of public officials can be repackaged as a personal safety matter, democratic scrutiny itself is placed at risk.” Sehr compiled an almost 500-page dossier of posts from Hurlston’s Stonnington Council Watch Facebook page and other messages that she said had escalated to personal harassment. The judge accepted Sehr (pictured) felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but found her fear wasn’t the same as a fear for her safety. Ruby Alexander Clayton said Hurlston was “an enormous nuisance” to Sehr and some of the posts were hurtful, including one that accused the mayor of using her mother’s death to avoid questions. She accepted the mayor felt unfairly targeted and fearful about further posts, but added: “That sort of fear, however, is not the same as a fear for one’s safety.”

Advertisement

The judge ultimately found Hurlston’s posts were published without malicious intent and thus an intervention order could not be made. The previous order restricted Hurlston’s online commentary towards Sehr and barred him from coming within two metres of her. “Mr Hurlston may not abide by a journalistic code of conduct in relation to fair and balanced commentary,” Clayton said. “This does not mean he is not entitled to the protection afforded by [the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act].” She added: “It is permissible for Mr Hurlston to publish, filled with ill-will, animosity, spite and hostility if the actuating motive for the publication is not improper.” Clayton said the images Hurlston posted of Miss Piggy and a cartoon of a stereotypical housewife could be seen as demeaning or derogatory towards Sehr.

Advertisement

Hurlston said the Miss Piggy image referred to Sehr as a “muppet” as it was a common derogatory term in politics, and it was not intended to attack her appearance. Related Article City life Mega merger not the answer to funding shortfall, councils say The judge acknowledged Sehr felt humiliated, but was not persuaded the image was primarily motived by something other than Hurlston’s political opinion that the mayor was “not up to the job”. The judge also said the housewife cartoon was not substantially different from thousands of other political caricatures. “Women in public life generally, and politics in particular are often unfairly targeted in relation to their appearance,” Clayton wrote.

“While one might bemoan this sorry state of affairs it is not a state of affairs that the act was intended to address.” Sehr told The Age she was awaiting further legal advice after Friday’s decision. Luis Guzman grew up with Australia in his sights. After watching the film Kangaroo Jack as a six-year-old in Guatemala, he told his mother the country would one day be his home. At 18 he came down under to travel. At 28 he enrolled in a master’s degree in event management at the UTS Business School. Luis Guzman moved to Sydney from Guatamala to study. “The quality of life, the opportunities that I can have here … I think it’s really nice.” Wolter Peeters Now in his final semester, Guzman has high hopes for the future. “I know that in Australia, if I work hard and I put effort in, I can achieve more.” Related Article Updated

Immigration Labor’s tough new migration rules target backpackers, foreign students and overstayers Guzman is one of hundreds of thousands of international students who come to Australian universities to pursue their dreams. Since 2021, international student enrolments at Australian universities increased by 46.2 per cent – from 314,619 to 460,090. Those numbers have been a primary target of the federal government’s plans, revealed on Thursday, to curb net migration from about 300,000 to 225,000 next year. It aims to curb the number of international students by targeting visa hopping and by reducing the influx of family members.

The most popular broad field of study for international students enrolled in Australian universities was management and commerce, accounting for 120,136 enrolments in 2026. Information technology ranked second, followed by society and culture. The most studied management and commerce disciplines were business and management (61,222 enrolments), followed by accounting (14,566 enrolments). Speaking before the migration changes were unveiled, International Education Association of Australia chief executive Phil Honeywood said those degrees had broad appeal to international neighbours, offering in-demand skills taught in a native English setting. “The overwhelming number of overseas students doing such courses come from family businesses where the parents would like their child to learn business practices in a native English-speaking country, and … go home to run the family business or to start in a larger corporation.”

“If I talk with my friends who are international students, I think they are going to feel anxious about their futures,” he said. While management and commerce has maintained its position as the most-studied field by international students over the past five years, its contribution to enrolments dropped by 21.5 per cent. Honeywood says this coincides with the removal of finance and accounting from the Australian government’s skills-in-demand list. title: Five years, millions of dollars: The battle to fix a defective Sydney building
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Andrew and Lisa Cook moved into their new apartment in Baulkham Hills on December 12, 2020, they thought they were getting the dream: a modern unit, a sprawling balcony with views of the city skyline and access to shops at the base of their building. Just 23 days later, the dream became a nightmare: the company that developed the building collapsed. Ten months after that, the state’s building regulator identified serious defects in the development, including one that was labelled a “hazard to human life”. The Cooks were shocked. They didn’t know who would be responsible for fixing the defects, and what it meant for their new home. “[We were] a bit scared because they didn’t know what was going to happen at the time,” Lisa said. Andrew and Lisa Cook on their balcony, which is still being repaired. Jessica Hromas Known then as the Modena, the four-tower project was developed by Hills Shoppingtown Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of Dyldam Group – once one of NSW’s biggest apartment builders before it collapsed with debts of half a billion dollars. There were 230 apartments and plans for a retail precinct in a project designed to combine luxury and comfort. When the receivers for the development and the building regulator visited the site, they found it was far from that vision. In addition to non-compliant waterproofing, an awning in danger of collapse, balconies without water overflows, the glass elevator – designed as a key feature for the project – had already rusted and was leaning slightly.

Advertisement

For five years, the Cooks and a handful of other residents have lived in a construction zone as millions of dollars were funnelled into rectifying defects. The scale of the work is so significant that the Cooks have lived in another unit since January while work on their own apartment continues. “There’s been a lot of noise for quite a few years, so that’s sort of a bad thing, but I keep thinking they’re doing it, they’re fixing it, it’s not costing us any money,” Andrew said. The Baulkham Hills building, formerly known as the Modena. Jessica Hromas. The stairs to the lower lever remain fenced-off while work continues. Jessica Hromas “We’re one of the fortunate buildings in Sydney.” Buying a home with defects is not an uncommon experience in NSW. Building Commission NSW ordered major developer Bathla Group, which entered voluntary administration last month, to fix serious defects in two of its developments. It’s left those who purchased off the plan uncertain if they would ever move in. So when developers collapse owing millions of dollars, how do you fix a defective building?

Advertisement

The $70 million fix When McGrathNicol was appointed the receiver of the Modena development in 2021, partner Jason Ireland said they were told the project was 95 per cent complete. But what was anticipated to be a quick fix soon became a mammoth project that would take years and $70 million to rectify defects – bringing the total cost of completing the development to $185 million. Ireland describes the project as being a bit like an onion, “in that when you peeled back [layers], you found more problems that made you cry,” he said. More than 60 defects were found throughout the four buildings. McGrathNicol’s Jason Ireland said it has cost $70 million dollars to fix the defects left behind by the original builder. Jessica Hromas Fixing the overflow holes in balconies was considered a simple job. Then the tiles began to be removed, and a new problem appeared: No one could identify what waterproofing material had been used. Ireland said it was clear it was a non-compliant product. “We eventually got to the conclusion that the only way to actually get the sign-off in the end was to rip up the balconies, replace all of the waterproofing, and replace all of the tiling, which is a lot because there’s over 200 apartments,” he said. Through it all, the four buildings have been partially occupied. In a Tetris-like process, residents had to be moved from their apartments to another in the development to allow for each to be rectified in turn.

Advertisement

When the Herald visited last month, work was continuing. The elevator had been replaced, the stairs to the lower level remained fenced off and some balconies – including the Cooks’ – were still under repair. The new elevator, which the replaced the original, rusted one. Jessica Hromas Ireland said there is light at the end of the tunnel, with 90 per cent of the defects fixed. Building Commission NSW lifted its building work rectification and prohibition order for the development, which has been rebranded as “Alfresco Quarter”. An interim occupation certificate remains in place. In May, the commission accepted a voluntary undertaking from McGrathNicol, which will provide additional independent oversight of the development. About 50 per cent of the apartments have now been sold, and the empty retail precinct has been acquired by property services provider Mintus. The lower level will have a gym, and cafés and restaurants are planned for the upper level. Work will be completed next year. An artist’s impression of what the cafe at the Baulkham Hills development would look like. Alfresco Quarter Ireland said: “The silver lining to the cloud is that if you buy a property in this building, you know it’s been through the highest of verification standards by the building commissioner’s team. They have been through it with a fine tooth comb.

Advertisement

“Some of the people [living] here have been to hell and back, but importantly, back.” The lucky ones Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it staves off liquidation It’s been a difficult, drawn-out process for the Cooks, but they’ve remained positive and hope to move back into their own apartment before the end of the year. “This is our forever home,” Andrew said. “And the tiles they put down are much nicer than the old ones.” Despite the stress it’s caused, the Cooks consider themselves lucky; unlike many other owners living in buildings with defects built by collapsed developers, the family didn’t have to fund the repairs. At the Vicinity complex in Canterbury, owners are still picking up the tab after major structural defects were discovered in parts of the 276-apartment complex, which was built by collapsed developer Toplace.

title: Fed up with taxes, Aussies are following Adrian Portelli to Dubai. The ATO is watching
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaDubai Fed up with taxes, Aussies are following Adrian Portelli to Dubai. The ATO is watching Angelica Snowden September 19, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adrian Portelli’s rationale for moving to Dubai, at least in his telling, is pretty simple. Australia is “chasing away success”, according to the Melbourne-born billionaire, and entrepreneurs like him will keep leaving with one-way tickets because of exceedingly harsh tax settings. “I don’t trust the government,” Portelli told Karl Stefanovic in a new episode of the broadcaster’s controversial podcast. “They’ve really come down on me. Billionaire Adrian Portelli has moved to Dubai, and told Karl Stefanovic he doesn’t “trust” the Australian government. AAP “I’ve had regulatory issues to ATO [Australian Taxation Office] issues, and I just can’t handle it.” Portelli has more than 1 million followers on social media and in August, he told them he was relocating to the Middle East, in response to this year’s federal budget, and its sweeping changes to capital gains and property taxes that sparked warnings that innovation in Australia would be stifled.

Advertisement

Critics, including other young entrepreneurs, united to lobby against changes to capital gains taxes for business. Broadly, Portelli and Stefanovic’s discussion suggested wealthy Australians could vote with their feet and shift their lives and their businesses overseas, to countries where the regulatory burden is less prohibitive. Related Article Federal budget How a meme war with tech bros derailed Labor’s budget narrative Portelli is doing so and more are intending to follow his lead, according to Victoria Wells, a Melbourne lawyer who started her firm, Ape Law, in the United Arab Emirates in 2022. Last month, Wells and partner Stephan Roberto, along with Bali-based influencer couple Matt Cameron and Felicity Morgan, launched the business “Project Get Out”, to capitalise on Australians – particularly those working in tech – wanting to shift overseas. They received 1000 inquiries shortly after launching – just as Portelli went viral for his move.

Advertisement

But experts warn that it is not always straightforward for relocating Australians to cash in on lower tax rates. Deakin Business School lecturer Dr Kerui Zhai said Australia’s higher personal income taxes and the changes to capital gains tax were among the incentives for entrepreneurs to relocate to the UAE, where they could obtain “significant tax savings”. But he pointed out that companies with income largely derived from Australia would “probably still be subject to Australian corporate tax”. Dubai has been competing with Singapore and Bali to entice expats overseas, expats say. Bloomberg About 25,000 Australians live and work in Dubai. Expats from across the world comprise about 88 per cent of the broader UAE population, which hovered at 11 million in 2025, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. While some have left due to the war in Iran, Professor Sunita Jogarajan, from the University of Melbourne Law School, said there was a long-term increase in Australians making the move since the pandemic, with destinations such as Bali and Singapore also spruiking tax benefits to attract expats.

Advertisement

“I can see it from the cases going through the Administrative Review Tribunal. I have been in tax more than 20 years. There just was not as many [cases related to Australians’ tax status] as before,” Jogarajan said. Tribunal records show the ATO has indeed been pursuing Australians living overseas deemed to be tax residents to pay their share, regardless of where they are. ‘I’ve had regulatory issues to ATO issues, and I just can’t handle it.’ Adrian Portelli Engineer Trong Quy sought a refund of $524,943.29 from the tax office for the period between 2016 and 2020 because he claimed Dubai was his primary place of residence. But in March last year, he lost his final bid for a refund, as the tribunal ruled he was a resident of Australia. The tribunal judgment said: “Despite not treating Australia as his home in the relevant years, the applicant maintained connections with Australia that are objectively inconsistent with his ‘abandoning’ residence in Australia and making Dubai a ‘permanent’ (in the sense of not temporary) home.”

Advertisement

These connections included that Quy’s family home was in Perth, where his wife and daughters lived. Quy also acknowledged that he left other personal belongings in Australia “including winter clothing (not required in Dubai’s climate) and two guitars that he had been restoring”. Related Article Gambling Adrian Portelli’s giveaway business to be outlawed Earlier this year, oil and gas executive Ragnar Bulie won against the ATO, after it sought to make him pay tax on income earned in Singapore between 2018 and 2022. Bulie, who is from Norway and owns property in Australia, lived in Singapore during that time while his wife and children resided in Australia. He was earning about $700,000 per year, according to the tribunal’s judgment. “Mr Bulie’s economic and personal relations to Singapore were, in composite, stronger than his economic and personal relations to Australia during the relevant period,” the tribunal ruled.

Advertisement

Portelli earned his estimated $1.44 billion fortune – according to The Australian Financial Review’s Rich List – from his subscription-based lottery business that recently expanded into petrol stations. Before his move overseas, the federal government unveiled legislation to outlaw his business model. Discussing his plans for a new business, a “streamlined way for Australians to import goods”, Portelli told Stefanovic “they froze my accounts”. “I couldn’t pay my wages, I couldn’t pay staff. I couldn’t pay my bills. They just froze it all,” he said, without explaining exactly who took the action against him. “My accountant said he has never seen anything like this. He genuinely said they have abused their power.

Advertisement

“They are chasing young entrepreneurs, very talented [Australians]. People of wealth and success are moving. They are fleeing.” Related Article Petrol prices Discount fuel and cash giveaways: How Adrian Portelli’s business works In the UAE, corporate income is taxed at 9 per cent and there is no personal income tax. In Australia, companies pay a tax rate of at least 25 per cent, and personal income rates top out at 45 per cent for the most well-paid Australians. Jogarajan, who acknowledged she did not know how Portelli’s business was structured, suggested the billionaire could still be treated as an Australian resident for tax purposes. “Foreign residents are taxed in Australia on any money they make in Australia,” she said. “That’s the kind of thing people pay lawyers to get advice on.”

Advertisement

Portelli did not respond to a request for comment. Speaking generally, Jogarajan said: “You really need to move and have a home overseas and not have those connections to Australia. “One of the big issues is if the family doesn’t move. The individual might be in Australia for a short number of days, say 30 or 60 days, and not typically be considered a resident here, if their family and children are still here.” Crypto lawyer Victoria Wells began a business, “Project Get Out”, to advise Australians moving to Dubai. Wells’ “Project Get Out” seeks to advise on relocation and tax residency issues for Australian founders, investors and high-net-worth families. She said the venture wasn’t “about engineering arrangements to avoid Australian tax”.

Advertisement

“Tax is legitimately one consideration in that decision, alongside lifestyle, family, business opportunity, regulation and access to markets – but it shouldn’t be the decision itself. I often say that tax should be one coordinate on the map, not the compass,” Wells said. Wells contemplated her exit from Australia years before the latest military action in the Middle East. After the price of crypto crashed in 2022, which coincided with news that the asset would no longer be treated as a foreign currency, and hit with capital gains tax in Australia, Wells said many founders and crypto firms left Australia. Wells and partner Stephan Roberto. “That was really the writing on the wall for me. My friends and my peers were leaving. I was like, OK, I have to figure this out. Are there going to jobs in crypto in Australia? No. Are there going to be clients in crypto in Australia? No, they are also leaving,” she said. During the past 3½ years operating her Dubai-based law firm, Wells specialises in financial services, international arbitration and crypto. She said the business had reported exponential growth from clients seeking to domicile their companies in the UAE.

Advertisement

Since launching “Project Get Out”, Wells said she continued to clock 200 inquiries a day. “Adrian Portelli announced his departure from Australia, it was picked up and got a lot of press. [Meanwhile], the work that I do, naturally puts me front and centre for a lot of Australians looking at making an exit to the UAE specifically,” she said. Morgan, one of her Australian co-founders, is an influencer who moved to Bali two years ago. Her business, Felicity Morgan Coaching, was liquidated last September. According to the liquidator’s report in December, Morgan owed the ATO $774,118.65 in unpaid liabilities. The report also said Morgan received a director’s loan from the company for $1.08 million, which the liquidator requested be repaid. Morgan said: “The current status is incorrect, however, things take time to show on the system.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Before training Bentley to be her support dog, Angel Oliver was living with a constant state of severe anxiety, and dealing with a rollercoaster of health issues. But now Oliver, who struggles with anxiety, ADHD, autism and autoimmune issues, has found huge solace in having Bentley the golden digger by her side. Angel Oliver describes Bentley as her ‘soul dog’. Neesha Sinnya “I couldn’t do so many of the everyday things others take for granted, like not being able to stand in a packed lift or walk through a crowded building without a panic attack,” she said. “I told a [dog] trainer that I can’t go to the supermarket because I get panic attacks, and they said: ‘You know if you have a disability you could actually train him and apply for him to be your assistant animal?’”

Advertisement

Oliver is telling her story at Darvella Patisserie in Bulimba. The cafe’s owner, Giorgina Venzin, explains to this masthead that the pair are regulars, with Bentley a particular fan of her puppacinos. Related Article Pets Can having a dog boost your longevity? Oliver originally got Bentley as a pet – “he was simply my puppy” – but as she experienced a traumatic event, and her health began to unravel, she came to rely on him more and more. After a year of training with MindDog Australia, Bentley is now a certified support dog. He helps Oliver through companionship, deep pressure therapy and even glucose monitoring.

“He helps just by being there and helping me deal with my health issues,” she said. The Brisbane Dog Friendly page existed before Oliver came to the city, with a mission of highlighting dog-friendly venues around the city. Once she moved up from Melbourne in 2024 and took over the account, Oliver worked to turn it into an even stronger community. “When I first moved to Brisbane I had no friends,” she said.

Bentley the golden digger can vouch for Darvella Patisserie’s puppacinos. title: V’landys receives unanimous support from clubs and states to become NRL executive chair
text:
Advertisement

The final hurdle has been cleared for Peter V’landys to become the NRL’s first executive chairman after club chairs offered their unanimous support for the move. The chairs of the clubs and state leagues took part in a phone hook-up on Saturday morning to discuss the ascension of V’landys to the new role. While Melbourne chair Matt Tripp and Wests Tigers counterpart Barry O’Farrell sent their apologies, all other officials backed the move during a half-hour conversation that began at 10:30am. Peter V’landys will become the NRL’s first executive chairman. Oscar Colman The appointment is expected to be rubber-stamped at a board meeting of the Australian Rugby League Commission scheduled for Wednesday. The role will give V’landys unprecedented control over the game, but the club and state heads feel there are sufficient guardrails in place to ensure protections. His tenure will be for an initial three-year term, a move V’landys himself proposed to ensure good governance.

Advertisement

If there is a dispute between V’landys and the clubs and states, they will be able to negotiate with a lead independent director who will be tasked to help resolve the impasse. While that role won’t be filled until V’landys ascends to his position, sources not authorised to speak publicly said ARL commissioners Peter Beattie and Gary Weiss are the leading contenders. Peter V’landys presents the minor premiership to Penrith earlierr this month. Getty Images Once V’landys takes the job, he will set a date to finish at Racing NSW, where he has been the chief executive for 22 years. V’landys is becoming executive chairman without calling a vote of clubs and states to amend the game’s constitution, which states that commissioners cannot be the CEO or an employee. Instead, he is relying on clause 53 of the document, which allows for the creation of other positions “from time to time” which can be occupied by members of the commission.

Advertisement

The sidestepping of constitutional change could be tested in court, but the unanimous support he received on Saturday suggests the key stakeholders have confidence in the direction V’landys is leading the game. The meeting was convened by South Sydney Rabbitohs chair Nick Pappas, who has been liaising with V’landys and the Commission about the move. “There was broad consensus among the clubs and the states,” Pappas said. “We have no objection to Peter taking that position – in fact we welcome it … There are some issues that require clarification in relation to guardrails around the position to ensure governance at the highest level, which is what Peter wants as well. “We are not at cross purposes on this … there is nothing that would act as an obstacle to him taking up that position.” V’landys has been acting as NRL chief for the past two months, having taken four months long-service leave from Racing NSW to fill the gap when Andrew Abdo departed for Tennis Australia.

Advertisement

Another perspective Analysis

NRL 2026 The 10 key issues V’landys must address as NRL’s first executive chairman He has cast a large shadow as chairman since his appointment in 2019, but will now permanently direct day-to-day operations as well as heading up the commission. It is a rare occurrence in Australian sport, where there is generally a separation of powers between the management and the board. The title provides V’landys even greater authority than the heads of US sports such as NBA commissioner Adam Silver and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, who are answerable to team owners. His elevation to executive chairman has raised governance concerns with some in the game, not about V’landys personally, but about a single figure wielding such control.

title: Trump, Denmark strike deal to shut Russia and China out of Greenland
text:
Advertisement

Updated WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Trump, Denmark strike deal to shut Russia and China out of Greenland Michael Koziol September 19, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Denmark, the United States and Greenland are expected to sign an agreement that will allow the US to increase its military presence in the Danish territory and ban adversaries such as Russia and China from building bases or making sensitive investments there. The agreement was simultaneously announced by all three parties and will be signed at the United Nations next week when world leaders converge on New York for the UN General Assembly’s high-level meetings. Greenlanders protest in front of the US consulate in the capital, Nuuk, in January. Getty Images US President Donald Trump claimed the deal as a significant win, after making Arctic security a key plank of his foreign policy agenda. But he frightened European allies with his demands for US control of Greenland, and his threats to perhaps take the Danish territory by force. Based on details provided by a US State Department official, the deal stops well short of giving the US control over Greenland, but expands American access and puts explicit, permanent restrictions on the presence of NATO adversaries.

Advertisement

It guaranteed the US “complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent”, the State Department official said, including permanent access, basing and overflight rights. Related Article Mining Trump has big hopes for Greenland – Australia just gave him a reality check “This agreement ensures the necessary US military presence in Greenland permanently, allowing the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as required.” Under the deal, a non-NATO country would not be allowed to build a military base or maintain a troop presence in Greenland, and only the US and its allies could make sensitive investments in Greenland. The US had raised concerns about Chinese investments in the territory, although experts have said these claims are inflated, with most of China’s purported projects there failing or never materialising.

Advertisement

“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” the State Department official said. Related Article Analysis

Immigration Denmark’s new Iron Lady wants more missiles and fewer migrants. Will Europe follow her lead? Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen welcomed what she described as a “great agreement” between the three parties, which would strengthen their collective security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The deal also recognised the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, she noted, as well as the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination. Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen branded the deal a “joyous” agreement that benefited all involved. His statement with Frederiksen noted the deal would need to be ratified by the relevant national parliaments, such as Greenland’s Inatsisartut.

Advertisement

Trump, meanwhile, called it a “dream come true” and said the US would immediately begin developing a large military presence in an appropriate part of the territory. “For over 100 years, [US] Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said on social media. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.” Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen (left) and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen in 2025. AP Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who played a key role in the negotiations, called it a “huge win” for the US and the American people. “Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he said.

Advertisement

“This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.” America’s military presence in Greenland was already enabled by the 1951 Defence of Greenland Agreement, which gave the US the ability to operate and maintain bases in certain areas by agreement. Vice President JD Vance, centre right, and Second Lady Usha Vance at Pituffik Space Base in Greenland in March 2025. AP The US currently has a base in Greenland, Pituffik on the territory’s northwest coast, which is utilised by the US Space Force and Air Force. There are only about 150 people permanently stationed at the base, down from 6000 at the peak of the Cold War. Several diplomats played down the significance of the new agreement, noting that while the full text was yet to be revealed, it did not appear radically different to existing arrangements.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

World politics Trump wanted Canada as the 51st state. He ended up pushing it towards the EU Michael McFaul, a former US ambassador to Russia under Barack Obama, said it appeared that Trump had “reaffirmed the security relationship we already had” with Denmark, “but he’s trumpeting it as some radical breakthrough”. “Fits a pattern, of course,” McFaul wrote on X. “But if it ends this nonsensical talk about planning to annex Greenland, that’s progress.” Daniel Shapiro, a former US ambassador to Israel, now a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank, said: “Chances are it’s a nothingburger dressed up to give Trump a ladder to climb down off the limb he stranded himself on.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. title: Albanese arrives in US for UN summit and big tech talks
text:
Anthony Albanese has arrived in California ahead of talks with tech giant Apple and an online safety push at the United Nations.

The prime minister landed in San Jose on Saturday morning AEST, for the first part of a week-long visit to the United States and was greeted by Australian ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty

Mr Albanese said Australia had been a world leader in online protections and was aiming to share the approach with others.

Anthony Albanese was greeted on the tarmac by Australian ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS)

"Other nations are reaching out, looking at the work that Australia has done," he told reporters upon arrival.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Australia has no greater friend than the US and tomorrow ... will be an important day looking at new technology and how we make sure we protect children in particular."

The prime minister is set to meet with former Apple chief executive Tim Cook at the tech giant's California headquarters on Sunday morning, Australian time.

The tech executive issued an open invitation to the prime minister to visit Apple following a conversation between the pair in June on Australia's world-first social media ban for under 16s.

Apple has said its parental control measures were in part inspired by Australia's ban.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Albanese will also see demonstrations of how the measures are put in place on Apple devices.

Digital safety will also form part of the prime minister's agenda when he later visits the United Nation's in New York for the forum's high-level week.

Efforts to force tech companies to remove harmful content online through a digital duty of care will be highlighted on the world stage, as will efforts giving social media users to opt out of algorithmic feeds.

Mr Albanese will meet with former chief executive Tim Cook at Apple headquarters. (EPA PHOTO)

National standards for AI companies, requiring them to be powered by renewable energy and data centres having an obligation to underwrite new power supply, is also expected to feature prominently in Australian addresses.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Albanese said countries around the world were grappling with AI technology as it rapidly expands.

"We need to make sure we shape its use in the interests of humanity, rather than allow it to shape us," he said.

"This is something that goes beyond national boundaries and that's why it requires discussion at the multilateral level."

The week-long visit to the UN will also involve Australia increasing lobbying efforts for a seat on the body's security council.

Australia is bidding to become one of the 10 non-permanent members of the 15-seat council for a two-year term in 2029 and 2030.

A vote for the positions won't take place until 2028.

Anthony Albanese has told reporters the use of AI must be shaped in the interests of humanity. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS)

So far, Australia and Finland are the only countries that have put up their hand for the two spots available from the Western Europe and Others Group but two-thirds of UN members still need to endorse the role if no other countries come forward.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Albanese will also receive an Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award on the sidelines of the UN, recognising his role in promoting security and stability in the Indo-Pacific.

He will be one of four people to be recognised by the council, including Finnish President Alexander Stuff, Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali and Oscar nominee and Wicked actress Cynthia Erivo.

title: Big Aussie hit that almost never was turns 40
text:
Forty years ago an unassuming Aussie artist released a song that would go on to become one of that country's most recognisable hits, an unofficial national anthem that would redefine careers for decades to come.

It was 1986, Kylie Minogue made her debut on Neighbours, Crocodile Dundee was released and so was a 10-track album titled Whispering Jack that would go on to find global success.

An era of big, bold prints, big hair and mighty big power ballads.

John Farnham's You're the Voice was a mighty big power ballad that's remained an Australian classic over four decades.

John Farnham's You're the Voice was one such song that's remained an Australian classic that still gets belted out by new generations of Aussies in backyards, cars and pubs around the nation.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

But like many tales of glory, it was a song that almost wasn't.

One of its co-writers, Chris Thompson, a singer and guitarist with Manfred Mann's Earth Band, didn't want Farnham singing the tune after the pop star's success with doozies like Sadie (The Cleaning Lady). He thought Farnham "was a joke" in Australia.

But Farnham was driven and so was his manger Glenn Wheatley, who risked everything to establish the singer as a reputable solo artist in Australia.

The famous Aussie duo were working on Whispering Jack, they had put a band together and needed a final song to complete the album.

Composer David Hirschfelder recalls when You're The Voice became a No.1 hit people were queuing around blocks to see John Farnham perform at suburban pubs. Picture: David Hirschfelder

Musician and film composer David Hirschfelder was 26 years old at the time and had been recruited to join Farnham after they worked in the Little River Band together.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

He recalls You're The Voice stuck out when it landed on Wheatley's desk among hundreds of cassettes 40 years ago.

"I loved working with John, and I loved the man and the singer, I thought he was incredible," Hirschfelder said.

"We already had nine songs, we were one song short, and we were considering writing one and then this one turned up.

"We had no idea how (huge it would be). I mean, we all liked the song. It really leapt out at us as something very powerful, but you just never know with these things.

"You can't predict a hit."

Glenn Wheatley and Farnham were a great team. Picture: Supplied

Hirschfelder said a tight-knit team worked on the song in a studio, including himself an engineer, a producer and Farnham, but Farnham never discussed with them Taylor's disapproval.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Hirschfelder said it was Farnham's idea to add bagpipes to the song after panpipes, whistles and ocarinas didn't sound quite right.

"John said, 'Well, we've tried all those pipes. What about bagpipes?' Ross (producer Ross Fraser) and I looked at each other, 'Bagpipes, that's crazy'," he said.

"But then part of me said, 'You know, that could be fantastic'."

Hirschfelder met with bagpipe expert Ross Campbell and they worked out how they could change the song a little to suit the bagpipes.

"We had to shift the song when they came in, and the fact that we had to shift it up to another chord that was not in the original version suddenly made the whole song lift," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's almost like the bagpipes, just by being so demanding and specific, we had to go with them and it just lifted the song.

"Then Glenn Wheatley sent a demo of what we'd done and a rough mix of how it was going to sound with bagpipes and everything, and (the songwriters) said, 'Oh that sounds fantastic, yeah, please go ahead and release it'."

Hirschfelder said adding bagpipes to You're The Voice lifted the song. Picture: Mark Dadswell

Hirschfelder said the team tried to stay chill about You're The Voice becoming a hit.

"John had high hopes for it and really wanted it to work, as did I, but for me as a 26-year-old guy at the time, I was just going with the flow, seeing how it happened," he said of the song that was inspired by a 1985 anti-nuclear disarmament protest in London's Hyde Park.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It was the obvious choice for a lead single … back in the day, you would always lead with one track, and that seemed the obvious one.

"A lot of people really liked it in the broadcast world radio, but there was a few diehard, cool school rock people who didn't think John Farnham was, perhaps even dare I say, worthy of their all too groovy radio station.

"Soon everyone, even the ones who were initially sceptical, were playing it, and so that's what surprised us, how it crossed over from being a popular song to something that actually garnered industry credibility.

"It's become a classic now, and of course, we never ever dreamt of that."

The songwriters initially didn't want Farnham to sing their tune but were won over by the bagpipes and Farnham's huge voice. Picture: Supplied

Hirschfelder, who was the keyboardist in Farnham's backing band, said when they had the No.1 hit they were playing in suburban pubs with queues of people trying to get in to see it going around the block.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The promoters were all stunned, as were we, that we were doing these tours in tiny divey little pubs and that huge amounts of people were coming, people that wouldn't normally go to those venues were coming," he said.

"The reaction was genuine. I mean, there was genuine excitement, and then when it took off overseas, we ended up touring the following year.

"We arrived in Sweden, there were screaming girls and things that I would never have believed possible."

Music journalist Ian McFarlane said everyone loved singing You're the Voice at the top of their voice because Farnham sang the hell out of it. Picture: YouTube

Music journalist Ian McFarlane was a huge music fanatic in his 20s, writing about music and other things at the time and listening to lots of heavy guitar bands from Melbourne and Sydney during the '80s.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It was all happening in the '80s, oh yeah, good times," he said.

"Everyone knew about John Farnham, he'd kind of been in the nether regions at the time because he'd been a former teen pop idol who no one really cared about anymore.

"He'd just come out of the Little River Band, and it was like where does he go from there?

"But when he appeared with Whispering Jack and the single, everyone was just stunned at how good it was and how good he sounded because he always had that huge voice.

"His voice matched with that song definitely captured the imagination of record buyers."

Music Journalist Ian McFarlane authored the Encyclopaedia of Australian Rock and Pop. Picture: Rob Leeson.

McFarlane said You're The Voice had the big modern '80s production with drum machines, drum programming, the Fairlight synthesiser and the big, snappy beats.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"There was something about that song that certainly captured the times," he said.

"It's got that big adult-oriented rock sound and it's got the kind of Celtic rock edge with that crazy bagpipe solo in the bridge.

"I just love their bagpipe solos, a bit of AC/DC.

"It's such an ear-catching chorus, and that's the thing, everyone loves singing it at the top of their voice because John Farnham sings the hell out of it.

"It's that rallying cry, it's that you know we are all together; we're standing as one sort of consciousness.

"I've heard little kids absolutely singing that at the top of their voice as well, not teenagers or people in their 20s, little kids.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's got something that grabs you by the throat, and it says you've got to join in."

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd says You're The Voice is an Australian anthem. Picture: Supplied

Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) chief executive Annabelle Herd was a teenager living in Canberra at the time You're the Voice was released.

Farnham's Whispering Jack tour was the first live show the music boss attended.

"The reason the song hits home so much, and did at the time and continues to this day, I mean, John Farnham himself, it was a big comeback story," she said.

"As a teenager at that time, I didn't know about his previous career, so for me, he was like a new artist, but he was it.

"It was so huge. I mean, in the late '80s, obviously we had far fewer content and media platforms, so when something dominated in our culture, it really dominated.

"But this particular song seemed to even transcend that and its impact is long lasting."

Ms Herd said You're The Voice was absolutely an Australia anthem performed by an incredible and iconic Australian artist.

"It's obviously a great piece of music and a great recording, and his incredible voice, but it really just touches people because it just embodies that idea of standing up for what you believe in no matter how small your voice is, it can still change things," she said.

"It does it in a way that brings people together. A single voice coming together can change the world, it's inspiring and I was inspired when I first heard it.

"It makes you feel emotion every time you hear it, and you hear it a lot because it's performed a lot. It's very special."

Ms Herd said Farnham 'pretty much won every ARIA that was going' at the first awards night. Picture: Jonathan Ng

Ms Herd said You're The Voice was No.1 for seven weeks in Australia. It also went to No.1 in Germany and made the top five in Ireland, Switzerland and top six in the UK, Austria and Canada.

"It even got into the US charts, which was pretty incredible," she said.

"Whispering Jack had a pretty strong, clean sweep at the first ever ARIA Awards.

"John Farnham pretty much won every ARIA that was going in that very first ARIA awards.

"It had the success then, but since then it's obviously had incredible commercial success.

"It demonstrates that the power of an incredible song across our culture because there aren't many things that can cause people to feel the way that a really good piece of music or a really good recording of a song does.

"You're The Voice is the perfect example of that connection and how music can influence people, thinking and consumer behaviours."
